lessons.unit: R1-R8: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: units, scale and ratio
lessons.title: Converting standard and compound units
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does 1 m² not equal 100 cm²?
objectives: Convert between metric units of length, mass, capacity and time
Convert area and volume units
Convert compound units such as km/h to m/s, numerically and algebraically
successCriteria: All: convert lengths, masses and capacities
Most: convert areas, volumes and speeds
Some: convert compound units in algebraic expressions
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: converting g/cm³ to kg/m³ and m/s to km/h
lessons.smsc: Adab of precision: honest measurement and fair weights are stressed in the Qur'an (e.g. 55:9, 'give just weight and do not fall short in the balance').

keywords.def: the number you multiply or divide by to change units
a unit made from two others, such as km/h
a unit in the metric system such as m, kg, l

starter: Bismillah. Work out 3.5 km in metres.
Write 0.45 as a fraction in its simplest form.

teach.heading: The metric facts to recall
bullets: 1000 g = 1 kg, 1000 kg = 1 tonne
1000 ml = 1 litre, 1 cm³ = 1 ml
60 s = 1 min, 60 min = 1 h
teach.note: Quick-fire recall on mini-whiteboards. These must be known: no formula sheet is given in the GCSE. Ask which way you multiply when moving to a smaller unit (more of them, so multiply).

teach.heading: Converting areas and volumes

model.problem: Change 2.4 m² into cm².

teach.note: Draw a 1 m square split into 100 cm strips each way: 100 rows of 100 squares. Stress that the conversion factor is squared for area and cubed for volume (1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³).
bullets: Area: square the length factor
Volume: cube the length factor

teach.heading: The classic area error
teach.note: Sketch the metre square again. Ask pupils to explain in a sentence why 100 cannot be right. This is the big question: have two pupils answer it aloud.

teach.heading: Compound units: speed

model.problem: Change 90 km/h into m/s.

teach.note: Convert the top, then the bottom, separately. Show the shortcut: km/h to m/s divide by 3.6 and back multiply by 3.6, but insist they can derive it.
bullets: Convert top unit first
Convert bottom unit second

teach.heading: Hinge: speed

check.q: A cyclist rides at 5 m/s. What is this in km/h?
check.why: 5 m/s = 5 x 3600 m per hour = 18 000 m/h = 18 km/h. 0.3 divides by 60 only once; 1.8 divides by 10 wrongly; 300 is m/min.

teach.note: Whiteboards up on three. Probe anyone choosing 0.3: they have converted to minutes only. Re-teach the two-step method if over 20% wrong.

teach.heading: Algebraic units

model.problem: A car travels at v km/h. Write its speed in m/s.

teach.note: Higher-tier style. Replace numbers by letters but keep the method identical. Check with v = 90 gives 25. ANSWERS: practice: 3 600 000 cm³; 7800 kg/m³; 20 m/s; 50q/3 cm³ per second. exit: 50 000 cm²; 21.6 km/h. core: 600 000 m²; 9000 s; 10 m/s; 43.2 km/h. extend: 8400 g over 3500 cm² is 2.4 g/cm². stretch: (x/1000) ÷ (y/60) = 0.06x/y km/h; 15 km/h. homework: 2500 kg/m³; 30 m/s.

practice: Change 3.6 m³ into cm³.
Steel has density 7.8 g/cm³. Change this into kg/m³.
A train travels at 72 km/h. Give its speed in m/s.
A tap fills a tank at q litres per minute. Write the rate in cm³ per second.
independent: Core: a) 0.6 km² in m². b) 2.5 hours in seconds. c) 36 km/h in m/s. d) 12 m/s in km/h.
Extend: A sheet of metal has area 0.35 m². Its mass is 8.4 kg. Find the mass per cm² in grams.
Stretch: A runner covers x metres in y minutes. Write the speed in km/h in terms of x and y; then find it when x = 1500 and y = 6.
exit: Write 5 m² in cm².
A bike travels at 6 m/s. Give this in km/h.
Big question: Why does 1 m² not equal 100 cm²?
lessons.homework: Convert 2.5 g/cm³ into kg/m³, and a speed of 108 km/h into m/s. Write one sentence for each explaining your factor.
lessons.send: SEND: put the conversion table on the desk and use the 'top first, bottom second' two-line layout. EAL: sort the vocabulary 'per', 'compound', 'convert' with pictures. Stretch: convert pressure, N/m² to N/cm².

lessons.unit: R1-R8: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: units, scale and ratio
lessons.title: Scale factors, scale drawings and maps
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a 20 cm map show a whole town?
objectives: Use a map or plan scale given as a ratio or as '1 cm to 5 km'
Convert between map length and real length
Use scale factors for scale diagrams and models
successCriteria: All: find a real length from a map length
Most: find a map length from a real length and write a scale as a ratio
Some: use a scale for areas and for mixed units
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: map reading with 1:25 000 Ordnance Survey maps
lessons.smsc: Social: travellers in Islamic history relied on maps and measured distance; accuracy serves truthfulness (sidq).

keywords.def: the ratio of a length in a drawing to the real length
the multiplier that takes one size to another
a drawing with all lengths in the same ratio to the real object

teach.heading: Reading a scale
bullets: 1:25 000 means 1 cm on the map is 25 000 cm real
Scale '1 cm to 5 km' becomes 1 : 500 000
Always use the same units on both sides
Multiply to go to real life, divide to go to map
teach.note: Establish the direction rule: map to real is multiplying by the scale factor. Ask: what does 1:25 000 tell us about the map compared with the land? (map is much smaller).

teach.heading: Map to real life

model.problem: On a 1:25 000 map, two mosques are 4.2 cm apart. Find the real distance in km.

teach.note: Slow through the unit chain cm, m, km. Pupils often stop at 105 000 and write it as km. Ask for an estimate first: 4 cm x 0.25 km per cm is about 1 km.

teach.heading: Real life to map

model.problem: A hall is 12.5 m long. A plan uses scale 1 : 250. Find its length on the plan.

teach.note: Reverse the operation: divide. Write the scale as 1 cm : 2.5 m, which gives 12.5 ÷ 2.5 = 5 as a check.

teach.heading: Hinge: direction

check.q: A model car has scale 1 : 20. The model is 21 cm long. How long is the real car?
check.why: 21 × 20 = 420 cm = 4.2 m. 1.05 cm divides instead of multiplying; 4.2 cm forgets to convert; 420 m is a unit error.

teach.note: Whiteboards. If 1.05 appears, ask 'is a car smaller than its model?'.

teach.heading: Areas on a scale drawing
teach.note: Higher: lengths scale by k, areas by k². Do the 1:500 row together: 5 m × 5 m = 25 m². ANSWERS: practice: 3.8 km; 1 : 50 000; 4.7 cm; 6 × 20 000² = 2 400 000 000 cm², which is 240 000 m². exit: 2.2 km; 20 cm. core: 8.3 km; 12 cm. extend: 18 cm to 900 cm gives 1 : 50; model height 15 cm. stretch: 1 cm is 4 km so 30 km is 7.5 cm. homework: 1 : 200 000; 7 km; 1 cm² on the map is 4 km², so 10 cm².
bullets: Areas use the scale factor squared

practice: A map has scale 1 : 50 000. Two villages are 7.6 cm apart. Find the real distance in km.
A river is 3.5 km long. Its length on a map is 7 cm. Write the scale as 1 : n.
A plan of a classroom uses 1 cm to 2 m. A wall is 9.4 m long. Find its length on the plan.
On a 1 : 20 000 map a field has area 6 cm². Find the real area in m².
independent: Core: 1 : 100 000 map: (a) 8.3 cm to km (b) 12 km to cm on the map.
Extend: A scale model of a mosque dome has diameter 18 cm. The real dome has diameter 9 m. Write the scale as 1 : n and find the model height if the real height is 7.5 m.
Stretch: Two towns are 18 km apart. On a map they are 4.5 cm apart. A new road will be 30 km. Find its length on the map.
exit: A map has scale 1 : 40 000. Find the real distance for 5.5 cm in km.
A car is 4.8 m long. A model is 1 : 24. Find the model length in cm.
Big question: How can a 20 cm map show a whole town?
lessons.homework: A map scale is 1 cm to 2 km. Write this as a ratio 1 : n. Then a lake is 3.5 cm long on the map: find its real length in km. Finally, find the area on the map of a 40 km² field in cm².
lessons.send: SEND: give a conversion ladder cm, m, km with arrows and colour multiply and divide steps. EAL: practise 'map length', 'real length', 'scale'. Stretch: find the area scale from 1:25 000 and ask the area of a farm in hectares.

lessons.unit: R1-R8: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: units, scale and ratio
lessons.title: Fractions of a quantity and ratio notation
lessons.bigQuestion: What is the difference between a fraction and a ratio?
objectives: Write one quantity as a fraction of another, including improper fractions
Use ratio notation and simplify ratios, including with units, fractions and decimals
Write a ratio in the form 1 : n
successCriteria: All: write one number as a fraction of another and simplify a whole-number ratio
Most: simplify ratios with different units and write 1 : n
Some: simplify ratios involving fractions and decimals and fractions above 1
lessons.crossCurricular: Cookery: recipes use ratios of ingredients
lessons.smsc: Gratitude: sharing a meal fairly so that everyone has enough.

keywords.def: compares the sizes of two or more quantities
a ratio with no common factor left
a fraction where the numerator is larger than the denominator

teach.heading: Fraction of another quantity
bullets: Put the part over the whole, in the same units
Then simplify the fraction
If the part is bigger, the fraction is above 1
teach.note: Examples: 90 cm of 1.2 m is 90/120 = 3/4. 35 of 20 is 35/20 = 7/4. Pupils must first convert to the same unit.

teach.heading: Mixed units

model.problem: Write 45 minutes as a fraction of 2 hours.

teach.note: Always convert to the smaller unit first. Ask: why not leave 45/2 ? (units differ).

teach.heading: Simplifying ratios with units

model.problem: Simplify 1.5 kg : 600 g, then write it as 1 : n.

teach.note: The 1 : n form divides by the first number so n can be a decimal. Compare with n : 1.

teach.heading: Ratios with fractions

model.problem: Simplify 2/3 : 5/6.

teach.note: Alternative: multiply both by 6 straight away. For decimals multiply by 10 or 100: 0.35 : 0.5 = 35 : 50 = 7 : 10.

check.q: Simplify 40 cm : 1.2 m.

practice: Write 36 minutes as a fraction of 1 hour in simplest form.
Write 75 g as a fraction of 0.6 kg.
Simplify 15 : 40 : 25.
Simplify 3/4 : 5/8 and 0.6 : 1.5.
independent: Extend: Write each of these in the form 1 : n: 4 : 10, 6 : 5, 250 ml : 1 litre.
Stretch: A class has 18 boys and 27 girls. (a) Girls as a fraction of the class. (b) Boys : girls in simplest form. (c) Girls as a fraction of the boys.
exit: Write 48 as a fraction of 30.
Simplify 1.2 litres : 450 ml.
Big question: What is the difference between a fraction and a ratio?
lessons.homework: A recipe uses 600 g flour and 0.45 kg sugar. Write flour : sugar in simplest form and as 1 : n. Then write the sugar as a fraction of the flour.
lessons.send: SEND: use bar models for fractions and ratios. EAL: pre-teach 'simplest form', 'numerator'. Stretch: if x : y = 2/3 : 5/4 find x/y.

lessons.unit: R1-R8: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: units, scale and ratio
lessons.title: Sharing in a ratio and multiplicative relationships
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we share fairly when the contributions are not equal?
objectives: Share an amount in a given ratio
Find an amount from one part or from a difference
Express a multiplicative relationship as a ratio or a fraction
successCriteria: All: share a quantity in a two-part ratio
Most: use a given share or a difference to find the total
Some: turn statements like 'A is 40% more than B' or '3a = 5b' into ratios
lessons.smsc: Justice ('adl): honouring the agreed shares of a partnership.

keywords.def: one share in a ratio
how much larger one share is than another
a relationship written using 'times' such as x = 2.5y

starter: Write 40% more than 50 as a number.

teach.heading: Share in a ratio

model.problem: Share £360 in the ratio 4 : 5.

teach.note: Draw a bar split into nine equal parts. Always check the shares add to the total. Use whole bar models for pupils who need them.

teach.heading: Using a difference

model.problem: Aisha and Bilal share money in the ratio 5 : 3. Aisha gets £30 more. How much is shared?

teach.note: Key idea: the data given tells you which parts to use. Another version: given the smaller share is £45 find the total. Ask pupils to say which parts the £45 corresponds to.

teach.heading: From words to ratios
teach.note: Row 2: A : B = 2.5 : 1, doubled to 5 : 2. Row 4 is the hardest: test with a = 5 and b = 3, since 3 × 5 = 5 × 3, so a : b = 5 : 3. The bigger multiplier goes with the smaller quantity.
bullets: Test with numbers to check the ratio

teach.heading: Hinge: 3a = 5b

check.q: If 3a = 5b, what is a : b?
check.why: Substitute a = 5, b = 3: 3×5 = 15 = 5×3. So a : b = 5 : 3. Pupils choosing 3 : 5 copy the numbers in order.

teach.note: Do the substitution test live. Link to R6: the larger coefficient goes with the smaller quantity. ANSWERS: practice: £100, £150, £200; 21 blue is 7 parts so 3 parts red = 9, total 30; 3 parts = 15 so 5 per part, 11 parts = 55; 3 : 5. exit: £36 and £48; difference is 3 parts = £36, so 1 part = £12 and Zayn has £24. core: 12, 36, 48; 7 : 4, A = 35, B = 20; concentrate 0.3 l; water for 0.3 l concentrate at 1:5 is 1.5 l. homework: ratio 2 : 3, so £110 and £165.

practice: Share £450 in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4.
Red and blue counters are in ratio 3 : 7. There are 21 blue. How many counters in total?
Sara and Yusuf share sweets in ratio 7 : 4. Sara has 15 more than Yusuf. How many sweets in total?
Write 'x is 60% of y' as the ratio x : y in simplest form.
independent: Core: Divide 96 kg in the ratio 1 : 3 : 4.
Extend: A is 75% more than B. Write A : B. If A + B = 55 find A and B.

Stretch: A drink mixes concentrate and water in the ratio 1 : 7. Alia makes 2.4 litres. How much concentrate is needed? Another drink is 1 : 5; she wants the same amount of concentrate. How much water?
exit: Share £84 in the ratio 3 : 4.
Tom and Zayn have money in ratio 5 : 2. Tom has £36 more than Zayn. How much does Zayn have?
Big question: How do we share fairly when the contributions are not equal?
lessons.homework: Fatima and Ibrahim invest £600 and £900 in a stall and share profit in the ratio of their investments. The profit is £275. How much does each get?
lessons.send: SEND: bar models and 'one part' flags. EAL: 'shared in the ratio', 'more than'. Stretch: three-way ratios from two-way ratios (a:b = 2:3, b:c = 4:5).

lessons.unit: R1-R8: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: units, scale and ratio
lessons.title: Proportion, ratio and linear functions
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one multiplier unlock a whole table of values?
objectives: Use the unitary method and multipliers
Recognise proportion as equality of ratios
Link direct proportion to y = kx and its straight-line graph through the origin
successCriteria: All: solve unitary and best-buy problems
Most: write and solve a proportion equation and find k in y = kx
Some: distinguish proportional from linear but not proportional relationships
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: ratio and proportion in density and recipes
lessons.smsc: Wisdom (hikmah): checking the price per unit so that we spend wisely and avoid waste.

keywords.def: two quantities that increase at the same rate so their ratio is constant
finding the value of one unit first
the fixed number k in y = kx

teach.heading: Unitary method

model.problem: 7 notebooks cost £5.60. Find the cost of 25.

teach.note: Present the same problem as a multiplier: 25/7 times larger. Show that C = 0.8n, so k = 0.8. Link to R8: the unit cost is the gradient of the graph.

teach.heading: Proportion means equal ratios
bullets: If y is proportional to x, then y/x is constant
y = kx where k is the constant of proportionality
The graph is a straight line through the origin
Equal ratios: 12 : 18 = x : 45 so x = 30
teach.note: Fill the table: x = 2, 5, 8 gives y = 6, 15, 24 with k = 3. Ask: what would y be at x = 0? (0). Proportion always passes through the origin.

teach.heading: Best buy

model.problem: A 750 g jar of honey costs £4.20 and a 1.2 kg jar costs £6.60. Which is better value?
steps: 1.2 kg jar is cheaper per 100 g

teach.note: Always compare the same units: price per gram or grams per pound. Discuss that value is not the only factor: need, storage, waste.

teach.heading: Hinge: is it proportional?

check.q: Which table shows y directly proportional to x?
check.why: Only the second keeps the same ratio y/x = 1.5. First is linear (y = 2x + 3) but not proportional; third is x squared; fourth has ratios 2/3, 1/2, 4/9.

teach.note: A taxi fare of £3 plus £2 per mile is linear but not proportional. Draw it to show why the line misses the origin. ANSWERS: practice: x = 30; 28 litres; 5 pens £0.65 each, 8 pens £0.625 so 8 for £5.00 better; k = 4 so y = 4x, y = 60. exit: £35.25; y/x = 2.5 each time. core: 1050 g, 700 ml; k = 1.75, x = 20; V = 4.5t. homework: £0.76 against £0.71 per 100 g, so the 2 kg pack is 5p cheaper per 100 g.

practice: A car uses 8 litres for 100 km. How many litres for 350 km?
Which is better: 5 pens for £3.25 or 8 pens for £5.00?
y is proportional to x and y = 24 when x = 6. Find y when x = 15, and write y = kx.
independent: Core: Recipe for 6 people needs 450 g rice and 300 ml water. Find amounts for 14 people.
Extend: y is proportional to x. When x = 8, y = 14. (a) Find k. (b) Find x when y = 35.
Stretch: A water tank fills at a constant rate. After 12 minutes it holds 54 litres. Write the volume V litres in terms of t minutes and sketch the graph.
exit: Find the cost of 15 kg if 4 kg cost £9.40.
The table x: 4, 10, 14 and y: 10, 25, 35. Show y is proportional to x.
Big question: How can one multiplier unlock a whole table of values?
lessons.homework: Two shops sell dates: 500 g for £3.80 and 2 kg for £14.20. Which is better value, and by how much per 100 g?
lessons.send: SEND: use a double number line and a ratio table. EAL: 'per', 'rate', 'proportional'. Stretch: explain why C = 3 + 2m is not proportional but is linear.

lessons.unit: R9-R12: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: percentages, proportion and compound measures
lessons.title: Percentages above 100% and percentage change
lessons.bigQuestion: Can something grow by more than 100%?
objectives: Use multipliers for percentage increase and decrease
Work with percentages above 100%
Calculate percentage change
successCriteria: All: find a percentage increase or decrease using a multiplier
Most: calculate percentage change and write a quantity as a percentage above 100%
Some: compare repeated percentage changes
lessons.crossCurricular: Business: profit, loss and growth in a market stall
lessons.smsc: Gratitude and honesty: stating profit and loss truthfully in trade.

keywords.def: the number you multiply by to apply a percentage change
change divided by original, as a percentage
the starting amount that the change is measured against

teach.heading: Multipliers
bullets: Increase by 15%: multiply by 1.15
Decrease by 15%: multiply by 0.85
130% of a number: multiply by 1.3
Percentages above 100% give multipliers above 1
teach.note: Build the pattern: 100% + 15% = 115% = 1.15. Ask what multiplier gives a 100% increase (2) and a 250% increase (3.5).

teach.heading: Percentage change

model.problem: A laptop rises in price from £480 to £528. Find the percentage increase.

teach.note: Highlight 'change over original'. Repeat with a decrease: £12 500 to £9 500 is 3000/12500 = 24% decrease.

teach.heading: More than 100%

model.problem: A stall sold 240 samosas last week and 360 this week. Write this week as a percentage of last week.

teach.note: Contrast 'is 150% of' with 'has increased by 50%'. Pupils often mix these.

teach.heading: Wrong original

misconception.wrong: A price goes from £40 to £52 so the increase is 12 out of 52: 23%

teach.note: Ask which value is the starting point. The original is the one the change is compared with: always divide by it.

teach.heading: Hinge: repeated change

check.q: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. Compared with the start, the final price is:
check.why: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 so 4% lower. The change is 20% of different amounts. Pupils choosing 'the same' think the percentages cancel.

teach.note: Use £100: £120 then £96. Use this to preview repeated change. ANSWERS: practice: 187; 25% decrease; 160% increase; 2700. exit: 20%; 78. core: 25% increase; 15% decrease; 150% increase. extend: 13%; overall 4% decrease because 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96. homework: 37.5% increase; £660. stretch: 1.4 × 0.75 = 1.05, a 5% increase.

practice: Increase 85 by 120%.
A price falls from £64 to £48. Find the percentage decrease.
45 grows to 117. Find the percentage increase.
A town of 2400 people grows by 12.5%. Find the new population.
independent: Core: a) 60 to 75: percentage change b) 200 to 170: percentage change c) 18 to 45: percentage change.
Extend: Raisa's salary rises from £28 000 to £31 640. Find the percentage increase.
Stretch: A shop raises prices by 20%, then offers 20% off the new price. Find the overall percentage change and explain it.
exit: Find the percentage increase from £35 to £42.
Work out 130% of 60.
Big question: Can something grow by more than 100%?
lessons.homework: A charity raised £640 at last year's Eid fair and £880 this year. Find the percentage increase. Next year they predict a 25% fall. Predict next year's total.
lessons.send: SEND: multiplier flash cards and a change/original/× 100 frame. EAL: 'of', 'by', 'from'. Stretch: share price rises 40% then falls 25%; overall change? Higher-only: comparing repeated percentage changes (the final hinge and the extend task).

lessons.unit: R9-R12: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: percentages, proportion and compound measures
lessons.title: Reverse percentages and simple interest
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we find the price before a discount?
objectives: Find the original amount after a percentage change
Calculate simple interest
Find the rate or the time from simple interest
successCriteria: All: find an original value after a given percentage change
Most: calculate simple interest and total
Some: find the interest rate or number of years
lessons.smsc: Islamic finance: interest (riba) is forbidden in Islam (Qur'an 2:275, 'Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba'); we learn the calculation to understand the system and the profit-sharing alternatives.

keywords.def: working back from a changed amount to the original
interest calculated only on the original amount
the amount of money at the start

starter: Find the multiplier for a 15% decrease.
Rearrange I = P × r × t to make t the subject.

teach.heading: Reverse percentages

model.problem: A coat is reduced by 15% in a sale. The sale price is £51. Find the original price.
steps: Sale price is 85% = 0.85 of the original

teach.note: Divide by the multiplier; do not add 15% to the sale price. Check: 0.85 × 60 = 51.

teach.heading: Adding the percentage back
teach.note: Ask why 15% of £51 is not the same as 15% of the original. The discount was calculated on the original price.

teach.heading: Hinge: reverse

check.q: After a 20% increase a price is £90. What was the original price?
check.why: 90 ÷ 1.2 = 75. £72 subtracts 20% of 90; £108 adds 20% again; £70 subtracts 20.

teach.note: Check on whiteboards. Ask pupils to show the check 75 × 1.2 = 90.

teach.heading: Simple interest

model.problem: Find the simple interest on £800 at 3.5% a year for 4 years.

teach.note: Interest is the same every year: it is a linear function of time. Relate I = Prt. Compare with the interest in Islamic finance: profit-sharing agreements rather than fixed interest.
bullets: I = P × r × t
Same amount each year

teach.heading: Finding the rate

model.problem: £500 earns £60 simple interest in 3 years. Find the annual rate.

teach.note: Rearranged: r = I / (P × t). Practise rearranging again for t. ANSWERS: practice: £125; £80; £180; 5%. exit: £120; £90. core: £8000; £1200; £400. extend: £5000; 4 years. stretch: 1.1 × 0.7 = 0.77, 308 ÷ 0.77 = £400. homework: £120 and £48 saving, because 40% is of the original £120, not of £72.

practice: A price including 20% VAT is £150. Find the price before VAT.
A coat is £56 after a 30% reduction. Find the original price.
Find the simple interest on £1200 at 2.5% for 6 years.
£750 becomes £825 in 2 years with simple interest. Find the annual rate.
independent: Core: a) After a 12% increase a value is £8960. b) After a 35% decrease it is £780. c) Simple interest on £2000 at 4% for 5 years.
Extend: A population falls by 18% to 4100. Find the original. £900 earns £108 simple interest at 3% a year: find the time.
Stretch: A price rises 10% and then falls 30% and is now £308. Find the original price.
exit: After a 25% increase a price is £150. Find the original.
Find the simple interest on £600 at 5% for 3 years.
Big question: How do we find the price before a discount?
lessons.homework: A sale offers 40% off. A prayer mat now costs £72. Find the original price and the saving. Explain why the saving is not 40% of £72.
lessons.send: SEND: use a bar model with 100% and the multiplier on a number line. EAL: 'reduced by', 'including'. Stretch: reverse a two-stage change.

lessons.unit: R9-R12: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: percentages, proportion and compound measures
lessons.title: Direct and inverse proportion: graphs and algebra
lessons.bigQuestion: If more people help, why does the job take less time?
objectives: Write and solve y = kx and y = k/x problems
Recognise graphs and tables of direct and inverse proportion
Apply proportion to real contexts and state assumptions
successCriteria: All: solve direct proportion problems using y = kx
Most: solve inverse proportion using y = k/x and identify graphs
Some: state assumptions and use proportion in unfamiliar contexts
lessons.smsc: Community (ummah): many hands make light work, e.g. preparing meals for a community iftar.

keywords.def: when one quantity increases, the other decreases so that their product is constant
the fixed value k
1 divided by a number

starter: Plot (2, 5) and (4, 10): what do you notice about the ratio y/x?

teach.heading: Two kinds of proportion
teach.note: Draw both sketches on mini-whiteboards. Ask for one real example of each: cost and number of items (direct), workers and time (inverse).

teach.heading: Direct proportion

model.problem: y is directly proportional to x. y = 18 when x = 4.5. Find y when x = 7.

teach.note: Always find k first and write the equation y = 4x. Then substitute. Show the answer on the graph.

teach.heading: Inverse proportion

model.problem: y is inversely proportional to x. y = 6 when x = 4. Find y when x = 10, and x when y = 1.5.
steps: y = k/x so 6 = k/4 and k = 24

teach.note: Check the product xy = 24 in both. Link to context: 6 builders take 10 days so 4 builders take 15 days (xy = 60), assuming all work at the same rate.

teach.heading: Hinge: inverse

check.q: y is inversely proportional to x. y = 8 when x = 3. What is y when x = 12?
check.why: k = 8 × 3 = 24, so y = 24/12 = 2. 32 treats it as direct proportion (x ×4 so y ×4); 11 subtracts; 0.5 is 6/12.

teach.note: Whiteboards. For anyone choosing 32 ask 'does y go up or down when x goes up?'.

teach.heading: Spot the proportion
teach.note: A: xy = 24 constant, inverse. B: y/x = 3 constant, direct. C: neither, y = x + 5. Pupils test both products and ratios. ANSWERS: practice: 60; 2; 24 minutes (equal flow); xy = 36 for each point. exit: 19.2; 7.5. core: 10; 7.5 and 60. extend: k = 300 so V = 4. stretch: k = 3, y = 3x², so 147. homework: 3 hours, assuming the same rate per person.
bullets: Test y/x then test x × y

practice: y is directly proportional to x. y = 35 when x = 7. Find y when x = 12.
y is inversely proportional to x. y = 5 when x = 8. Find y when x = 20.
8 taps fill a tank in 15 minutes. How long do 5 taps take? State your assumption.
The points (2, 18), (6, 6) and (3, 12) are on a curve. Show y is inversely proportional to x.
independent: Core: a) y ∝ x, y = 2.4 when x = 0.6; find y when x = 2.5. b) y inversely proportional to x, y = 3 when x = 10; find y when x = 4 and x when y = 0.5.
Extend: Gas pressure P kPa is inversely proportional to the volume V litres. P = 120 when V = 2.5. Find V when P = 75.
Stretch: y is directly proportional to x². y = 48 when x = 4. Find y when x = 7.
exit: y is directly proportional to x. y = 12 when x = 5. Find y when x = 8.
y is inversely proportional to x. y = 12 when x = 5. Find y when x = 8.
Big question: If more people help, why does the job take less time?
lessons.homework: 12 volunteers prepare 300 iftar boxes in 5 hours. How long would 20 volunteers take? What assumption have you made?
lessons.send: SEND: use a table and mark which row is multiplied or divided. EAL: 'directly', 'inversely', 'proportional to'. Stretch: y ∝ x² and y ∝ 1/x² (R13 next year). Higher-only: constructing y = k/x and y ∝ x² equations (stretch). Foundation: unitary method and tables.

lessons.unit: R9-R12: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: percentages, proportion and compound measures
lessons.title: Compound measures: speed, pay rates and unit pricing
lessons.bigQuestion: What does 'per' really mean?
objectives: Use speed = distance ÷ time and rearrangements
Convert time to decimal hours
Find average speed, pay rates and unit prices
successCriteria: All: calculate speed, distance or time
Most: calculate average speed for a two-part journey
Some: compare unit prices and use pay rates
lessons.smsc: Planning ahead (ihsan) and honesty about time when travelling in a group.

keywords.def: total distance divided by total time
a quantity per one unit of another, such as £ per hour
the price for one unit such as one kilogram

teach.heading: The speed triangle
bullets: Speed = distance ÷ time
Distance = speed × time
Time = distance ÷ speed
Convert minutes to hours before you divide
teach.note: Ask: what units? km/h with km and hours. Convert 24 minutes to hours: 24/60 = 0.4 h. Warn that 2 h 24 min is not 2.24 h.

teach.heading: Speed with time in minutes

model.problem: A bus travels 84 km in 1 h 45 min. Find its average speed.

teach.note: Alternative: 84 km in 105 min gives 0.8 km per minute = 48 km/h. Check by estimation: about 85 km in 2 h is about 42; slightly more.

teach.heading: Average speed

model.problem: Samir cycles 100 km at 50 km/h then another 100 km at 100 km/h (downhill, with the wind). Find his average speed.

teach.note: The average is not 75: total distance over total time. Cover this misconception with the 'half the time' discussion.

teach.heading: Hinge: time units

check.q: 2 hours 45 minutes in hours is:
check.why: 45/60 = 0.75, so 2.75. 2.45 is the common error of writing minutes as decimals; 2.25 is 15 minutes.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Show 1.5 h = 1 h 30 min as the anchor.

teach.heading: Pay rates and unit price

model.problem: Nadia earns £462 for 38.5 hours. Which is cheaper per kg: 2.5 kg of rice for £4.60 or 5 kg for £8.75?
model.answer: £12 per hour; 5 kg bag is cheaper

teach.note: Rates are everywhere: £ per hour, pence per unit, miles per gallon. Always divide by the quantity you want one of. ANSWERS: practice: 60 km/h; 3 km; 45 min; £12 per hour and £350. exit: 90 km/h; 1.25 h = 1 h 15 min. core: 7.5 m/s; 105 km; 54 km/h. extend: 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 h; 150/3 = 50 km/h. stretch: 15 km/h (take total distance 60 km). homework: 6 h; 450 ÷ 6.667 = 67.5 km/h.

practice: 210 km in 3 h 30 min: find the speed.
Walking at 4.5 km/h for 40 minutes: find the distance.
How long to travel 36 km at 48 km/h? Give your answer in minutes.
£384 for 32 hours' work: find the hourly rate; then find pay for 28 hours at £12.50.
independent: Core: a) 150 m in 20 s: speed in m/s b) 45 km/h for 2 h 20 min: distance c) 72 km in 1 h 20 min: speed.
Extend: 60 km at 40 km/h then 90 km at 60 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole journey.
Stretch: A cyclist goes half the distance at 12 km/h and the other half at 20 km/h. Find the average speed.
exit: Find the speed: 135 km in 1.5 hours.
How long to travel 100 km at 80 km/h? Give hours and minutes.
Big question: What does 'per' really mean?
lessons.homework: A coach journey of 450 km has an average speed of 75 km/h. How long does it take? The driver stops for 40 minutes in total; find the average speed including the stop.
lessons.send: SEND: provide the speed triangle and a time conversion table. EAL: pre-teach 'average', 'per', 'rate'. Stretch: harmonic mean of two speeds.

lessons.unit: R9-R12: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: percentages, proportion and compound measures
lessons.title: Density and pressure
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does a nail pierce wood while a flat hand does not?
objectives: Use density = mass ÷ volume
Use pressure = force ÷ area
Choose units and rearrange
successCriteria: All: calculate density or pressure
Most: find mass, volume, force or area by rearranging
Some: compare pressures on different faces and combine materials
lessons.smsc: Islamic Golden Age: al-Biruni, in the eleventh century, measured the densities of many metals and gems with remarkable accuracy.

keywords.def: mass per unit of volume
force per unit of area
the unit of force, N

starter: Work out the area of a rectangle 0.5 m by 0.3 m.
Rearrange D = M ÷ V to make M the subject.

teach.heading: Two formulae to know
bullets: Density = mass ÷ volume (g/cm³ or kg/m³)
Pressure = force ÷ area (N/m² or Pa)
Rearrange with the triangle
Keep units consistent: cm with cm, m with m
teach.note: These formulae are not given in the exam. Link: both are 'something per one unit': mass per cm³; force per m². Ask 'which unit tells you it is divided?'

teach.heading: Density

model.problem: A metal block has volume 250 cm³ and mass 1.95 kg. Find its density in g/cm³.

teach.note: Convert kg to g first. Show 7.8 g/cm³ = 7800 kg/m³ (links to the first lesson of this unit).

teach.heading: Mass from density

model.problem: Oak has density 700 kg/m³. Find the mass of 0.4 m³ of oak.

teach.note: Test unit sense: 0.4 m³ is a large block so 280 kg is reasonable.

teach.heading: Pressure and area

model.problem: A crate pushes down with a force of 600 N. Find the pressure on a face 1.5 m by 0.8 m and on a face 0.8 m by 0.5 m.

teach.note: Answer the opening big question: the nail has a small area. Ask why skis are wide.

teach.heading: Hinge: rearranging

check.q: A liquid has density 0.8 g/cm³. What is the mass of 250 cm³?
check.why: Mass = density × volume = 0.8 × 250 = 200 g. 312.5 divides instead of multiplying.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Use the triangle with the thing you want covered. ANSWERS: practice: 8400 kg; 3375 cm³ so 8 g/cm³; 30 000 N/m²; 10 000 N. exit: 7.8 g/cm³; 4000 N/m². core: 8 g/cm³; 420 g; 200 cm³; 3000 N/m². extend: total mass 1600 + 900 = 2500 g in 500 cm³, so 5 g/cm³. stretch: areas 200, 100, 50 cm² so pressures 1200, 2400, 4800 N/m²; greatest 4800 and least 1200. homework: 1.03 g/cm³ and 2.575 kg.

practice: Concrete has density 2400 kg/m³. Find the mass of 3.5 m³.
A cube of metal with side 15 cm has mass 27 kg. Find its density in g/cm³.
A force of 1800 N acts on 0.06 m². Find the pressure.
A pressure of 25 000 N/m² acts on 0.4 m². Find the force.
independent: Core: a) 960 g and 120 cm³: density b) density 1.2 g/cm³, volume 350 cm³: mass c) 540 g and density 2.7 g/cm³: volume d) 450 N on 0.15 m²: pressure.
Extend: 200 cm³ of metal A (8 g/cm³) is melted with 300 cm³ of metal B (3 g/cm³). Find the density of the alloy, assuming no change in volume.
Stretch: A brick weighs 24 N and measures 20 cm by 10 cm by 5 cm. Find the greatest and least pressure on a table.
exit: Find the density of 780 g of steel with volume 100 cm³.
Find the pressure from 200 N on 0.05 m².
Big question: Why does a nail pierce wood while a flat hand does not?
lessons.homework: One litre of milk (1000 cm³) has mass 1.03 kg. Find its density in g/cm³. Then find the mass of 2.5 litres.
lessons.send: SEND: use the triangle on a card and write units beside every number. EAL: 'density', 'pressure', 'force'. Stretch: convert N/cm² to N/m².

lessons.unit: R9-R12: Ratio, proportion and rates of change: percentages, proportion and compound measures
lessons.title: Ratios of lengths, areas and volumes
lessons.bigQuestion: If you double every length, why does the volume go up eight times?
objectives: Link a scale factor to ratios of lengths, areas and volumes
Use k, k² and k³
Find lengths from area or volume ratios
successCriteria: All: find area and volume ratios from a length ratio
Most: find a length ratio from an area or volume ratio
Some: solve problems with a model and the real object
lessons.smsc: Craft and precision: scale models of buildings such as mosques are made to proportion.

keywords.def: same shape, lengths in the same ratio
the multiplier between corresponding lengths
in the same position on each shape

starter: Work out the area of a square with side 4 cm.
Work out the volume of a cube with side 3 cm.

teach.heading: Scale factor k
teach.note: Ask pupils to draw a 1 by 1 square and a 3 by 3 square: 9 small squares. Then 1 cube and a 3 by 3 by 3 cube: 27 small cubes. This resolves the big question.
bullets: Lengths 3 : 1 means areas 9 : 1
Volumes 27 : 1

teach.heading: Volume from length

model.problem: Two similar bottles have heights 12 cm and 18 cm. The smaller holds 500 ml. Find the volume of the larger.

teach.note: Use k³ because volume is three-dimensional. Check by approximate: 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 is about 3.4.

teach.heading: Length from area

model.problem: Two similar rugs have areas 18 m² and 50 m². The smaller is 4.5 m long. Find the length of the larger.

teach.note: Square-root for lengths from areas, cube root for lengths from volumes. Simplify the ratio first so roots are exact.

teach.heading: Doubling the sides

misconception.wrong: Doubling all the lengths doubles the area and the volume.
misconception.right: Doubling all lengths multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8.

teach.note: Use a cube of side 2 cm turning into side 4 cm: area 24 to 96, volume 8 to 64.

teach.heading: Hinge: volumes

check.q: Two similar solids have lengths in the ratio 2 : 5. What is the ratio of their volumes?
check.why: 2³ : 5³ = 8 : 125. 4 : 25 is the area ratio; 2 : 5 is lengths; 6 : 15 multiplies by 3.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the area ratio too (4 : 25). ANSWERS: practice: 9 : 25 and 27 : 125; 2 : 3; scale factor 15 so 150 × 225 = 33 750 cm² = 3.375 m²; 4 : 7. exit: 64; 3 : 5. core: 16 : 100 = 4 : 25 and 64 : 1000 = 8 : 125; 800 cm³ × 125 000 = 100 m³. extend: volume ratio 1 : 8 so lengths 1 : 2 so labels 240 cm². stretch: areas 25 : 49, lengths 5 : 7, volume smaller 686 × 125/343 = 250 cm³. homework: 0.5 × 1600 = 800 m² and 0.02 × 64 000 = 1280 m³.

practice: Cubes with sides 3 cm and 5 cm: find the ratio of areas and volumes.
Two similar cones have curved surface areas 20 cm² and 45 cm². Find the ratio of their heights.
A statue is 3 m tall. Its model is 20 cm tall. The model has surface area 150 cm². Find the statue's surface area in m².
Two similar solids have volumes in the ratio 64 : 343. Find the ratio of their lengths.
independent: Core: a) Similar prisms have lengths 4 cm and 10 cm: ratio of areas and of volumes. b) A model ship scale 1 : 50 has volume 0.8 litres: find the real volume in m³.
Extend: Two similar jars hold 250 ml and 2 litres. Find the ratio of their heights. The label on the small jar has area 60 cm². Find the label area on the large jar.
Stretch: Two similar solids have surface areas 50 cm² and 98 cm². The larger has volume 686 cm³. Find the volume of the smaller.
exit: A length scale factor of 4: find the volume scale factor.
Similar shapes have areas 36 cm² and 100 cm². Find the ratio of their lengths.
Big question: If you double every length, why does the volume go up eight times?
lessons.homework: A model of a dome is built at scale 1 : 40. Its surface area is 0.5 m² and its inside volume is 0.02 m³. Find both for the real dome.
lessons.send: SEND: build with unit cubes or draw the 3 by 3 grid. EAL: 'corresponding', 'similar', 'scale factor'. Stretch: find the real volume from the model volume when only areas are given. Higher-only: area and volume scale factors k² and k³ (Foundation covers lengths only).

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Geometric vocabulary, notation and quadrilaterals
lessons.bigQuestion: How can words alone describe a shape exactly?
objectives: Use geometric notation and vocabulary precisely
Draw a diagram from a written description
Use the properties of quadrilaterals
successCriteria: All: name and describe quadrilaterals by their properties
Most: draw a sketch from a description and find missing angles
Some: identify a quadrilateral from several clues and justify the answer
lessons.smsc: Islamic art uses precise geometric constructions of squares, rhombuses and stars. Beauty arising from order and care (itqan).

keywords.def: meeting at a right angle
a line joining two non-adjacent vertices
cut exactly in half
a corner of a shape

starter: Bismillah. What do the angles in a triangle add up to?
What is the name of a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides?
State the order of rotational symmetry of a square.

teach.heading: Notation you must use
bullets: AB: the line from A to B
∠ABC: the angle at B between BA and BC
AB ∥ CD: parallel; AB ⊥ CD: perpendicular
Ticks mark equal sides; arrows mark parallel lines
teach.note: Give a quick sketch and have pupils read it back in notation. Stress that the middle letter in ∠ABC is the vertex. Many students write ∠BAC when they mean ∠ABC.

teach.heading: Quadrilateral properties
teach.note: Read down the diagonals column. Challenge: which shapes have equal diagonals? (square, rectangle, isosceles trapezium). Which have diagonals at 90°? (square, rhombus, kite). Pupils should build their own copy as retrieval practice.

teach.heading: Angles in a parallelogram

model.problem: ABCD is a parallelogram with angle DAB = 65°. Find the other three angles.
steps: Opposite angles are equal so angle BCD = 65°
Angles AD and AB are co-interior between parallel sides so angle ABC = 180° - 65° = 115°

teach.note: Always give a reason. A sketch helps: A bottom-left, B bottom-right, C top-right, D top-left. Check the total is 360°.

teach.heading: Draw from a description

model.problem: Draw triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm and angle ABC = 90°. M is the midpoint of AC. Find AC and BM.
steps: Draw AB 6 cm; at B draw a right angle; mark C 8 cm along
M is the midpoint so AM = 5 cm
M is equidistant from A, B and C so BM = 5 cm

teach.note: The fact that the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices is a Higher extension linking to the circle theorem in Year 11. Let pupils discover with a ruler.

teach.heading: Hinge: rhombus

check.q: Which statement is true for every rhombus?
options: The diagonals are equal in length
The diagonals bisect each other at right angles
check.why: The diagonals of any rhombus cross at 90° and bisect each other. Equal diagonals is a rectangle property; all right angles would make it a square.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Counter-example for A: a thin rhombus has one long and one short diagonal. ANSWERS: practice: ∠QPR; angle ADC = 110° because the kite is symmetrical about AC; rectangle; sketch. exit: square; 108°. core: rhombus and square; parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle and square; 5x + 20 = 180 so x = 32 and A = 96°. extend: draw PR = 8 cm, then arcs of radius 7 cm from P and 5 cm from R meet at Q. stretch: half diagonals 6 cm and 8 cm so the side is 10 cm and the perimeter 40 cm.

practice: Write in notation: the angle at P between PQ and PR.
In kite ABCD, AB = AD and CB = CD. Angle ABC = 110°. Find angle ADC and give a reason.
A quadrilateral has diagonals which are equal and bisect each other but do not meet at right angles. Name it.
Sketch an isosceles trapezium PQRS with PQ ∥ SR. Mark the equal sides and equal angles.
independent: Core: a) Which quadrilaterals have all four sides equal? b) Which have diagonals that bisect each other? c) A parallelogram has angle A = 3x and angle B = 2x + 20. Find x and the angle A.
Extend: Draw triangle PQR with PQ = 7 cm, QR = 5 cm and PR = 8 cm (SSS). Describe how you drew it.
Stretch: ABCD is a rhombus with diagonals AC = 12 cm and BD = 16 cm. Find the side length and the perimeter.
exit: Name the quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and cross at 90°.
A parallelogram has angle A = 72°. Find angle B.
Big question: How can words alone describe a shape exactly?
lessons.homework: Give three different properties that tell a rectangle from a rhombus. Then write a 'who am I?' clue set of three clues for a kite.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-drawn table of shapes and let pupils tick properties. EAL: pre-teach 'bisect', 'perpendicular', 'diagonal'. Stretch: prove that the diagonals of a rhombus meet at 90° using congruent triangles. Higher-only: the proof extension (stretch).

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Angle facts and parallel lines
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one known angle unlock all the others?
objectives: Use angle facts at a point, on a line and in triangles
Use alternate, corresponding and co-interior angles in parallel lines
Give reasons using correct vocabulary and solve with algebra
successCriteria: All: find missing angles with reasons
Most: solve multi-step angle problems in parallel lines
Some: set up and solve algebraic equations from angle facts
lessons.smsc: Precision in giving reasons: the habit of justifying every claim.

keywords.def: equal angles on opposite sides of a transversal between parallel lines
equal angles in matching positions
angles between parallel lines on the same side that add to 180°

starter: Angles on a straight line add up to what?
A triangle has angles 48° and 75°. Find the third angle.

teach.heading: Angle facts and reasons

head: Fact
Reason to write
rows: Angles on a line add to 180°
Angles round a point add to 360°
Angles in a triangle add to 180°
Exterior angle = sum of the two opposite interior angles

teach.note: Pupils copy the reason phrases into their books: marks are often given for correct reasons. Warn: 'Z angles' and 'F angles' are not reasons on their own in the exam: use alternate and corresponding.

teach.heading: Parallel lines

model.problem: PQ and RS are parallel. Line XY crosses PQ at X and RS at Y, with X above Y. Q and S are both to the right. Angle QXY = 62°. Find angle RYX, angle SYX and give reasons.
steps: Angle RYX = 62°: alternate angles (inside, opposite sides of XY)
Angle SYX = 180° - 62° = 118°: co-interior angles add to 180°
Check: RYX + SYX = 180° as angles on a straight line

teach.note: Draw the figure on the board: two horizontal parallel lines and a slanting transversal. Ask pupils to say it in words. Check with straight-line fact: R, Y, S are collinear.

teach.heading: Using algebra

model.problem: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two co-interior angles are (3x + 10)° and (2x + 30)°. Find x and the angles.

teach.note: If the angles had been alternate, we would use 3x + 10 = 2x + 30 giving x = 20. Compare the two equations side by side: the choice of fact decides the equation.

teach.heading: Hinge: co-interior

check.q: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are:
check.why: Co-interior (allied) angles lie between the lines on the same side of the transversal and add to 180°. Equal describes alternate and corresponding angles.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for a sketch with the C shape.

teach.heading: Exterior angle

misconception.wrong: The exterior angle of a triangle equals the adjacent interior angle.
misconception.right: The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles opposite it.

teach.note: Show with numbers: a triangle with 50° and 60° at the base gives an exterior angle of 110° and the third interior angle 70°. 180 - 70 = 110 also. ANSWERS: practice: 142°, 38°, 142° (reasons: straight line, vertically opposite); ABC = 65° (base angles equal and angle sum); other angle 55° (125 - 70); 4x - 20 = 2x + 30 so x = 25. exit: x = 25 (6x + 30 = 180); y = 68° (co-interior). core: 90 + 2x + 3x + 20 + x + 10 = 360 so 6x = 240 so x = 40; x + 2x + 5 + 3x + 7 = 180 so 6x = 168 so x = 28. extend: corresponding equal 3x + 5 = 50 so x = 15. stretch: exterior angle: 7y - 5 = 3y + 20 + 2y + 5 so y = 15.

practice: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 38°. Find the other three, with reasons.
In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle BAC = 50°. Find angle ABC, with reasons.
The exterior angle of a triangle is 125°. One opposite interior angle is 70°. Find the other.
Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. An alternate angle is (4x - 20)° and its pair is 2x + 30. Find x.
independent: Core: a) Angles around a point: 90°, 2x, 3x + 20 and x + 10. Find x. b) Triangle with angles x, 2x + 5 and 3x + 7: find x.
Extend: PQ ∥ RS. Angle at X (PQ) between XQ and the transversal is 50°, and angle at Y (RS) in the corresponding position is shown by (3x + 5)°. Find x and give the reason.
Stretch: In triangle ABC, D is on BC extended beyond C. Angle ACD = 7y - 5, angle BAC = 3y + 20 and angle ABC = 2y + 5. Find y.
exit: Angles on a line are x, 2x + 15 and 3x + 15. Find x.
Two co-interior angles are 112° and y. Find y and give the reason.
Big question: How can one known angle unlock all the others?
lessons.homework: Explain in words why the angles of a triangle add to 180° using a line parallel to one side.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-code alternate (blue), corresponding (green), co-interior (red). EAL: reason phrases on a sentence frame. Stretch: multi-stage angle chasing with an isosceles triangle between parallel lines.

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Angles in polygons and simple proofs
lessons.bigQuestion: Is there a rule that works for every polygon?
objectives: Find the sum of interior angles of any polygon
Use interior and exterior angles of regular polygons
Present a short proof of an angle result
successCriteria: All: use the angle sum of a polygon (n - 2) × 180°
Most: use exterior angles of regular polygons to find the number of sides
Some: construct a short proof with reasons
lessons.smsc: Islamic geometric patterns tessellate regular polygons, such as squares and octagons.

keywords.def: an angle inside a polygon at a vertex
the angle between a side and the extension of the next side
all sides and all angles equal

starter: Find the angle sum of a quadrilateral.
Find the angle sum of a pentagon by dividing into triangles.
A triangle has angles x, 2x and 3x. Find x.

teach.heading: Polygon angle sums
teach.note: Draw diagonals from one vertex of a hexagon to get 4 triangles. Ask pupils to complete the pattern and name the rule. Exterior angles of any polygon always add to 360°.
bullets: Sum of exterior angles is 360°
Interior + exterior = 180°

teach.heading: Regular polygons

model.problem: A regular polygon has an exterior angle of 24°. Find the number of sides and the interior angle.

teach.note: Working back: from interior angle 140° the exterior is 40° giving 9 sides. Pupils often try dividing 180 by something.

teach.heading: Hinge: nonagon

check.q: A regular polygon has interior angles of 140°. How many sides?
check.why: Exterior = 40°, and 360 ÷ 40 = 9. Choosing 8 comes from 360 ÷ 45 (regular octagon, interior 135°).

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the angle sum of this polygon as a follow up: 7 × 180 = 1260°.

teach.heading: Missing angle in a polygon

model.problem: A pentagon has angles 100°, 110°, 120°, 105° and x. Find x.

teach.note: Check by an estimate: angles near 108° on average (540/5), so 105° is sensible.

teach.heading: A short proof: angles in a quadrilateral
cycle: Draw diagonal AC splitting ABCD into two triangles
Angles in triangle ABC add to 180°
Angles in triangle ACD add to 180°
Angles at A and C of the quadrilateral are made of the triangle angles
So the quadrilateral's angles add to 360°
teach.note: Reading the cycle as a flow chart, pupils write each statement with the reason. Link to G6: a proof is a sequence of facts each with a reason. Ask them to repeat for the exterior angle theorem of a triangle. ANSWERS: practice: 1800°; 45° and 135°; 720 - 610 = 110°; exterior 18° so 20 sides. exit: 900°; 8. core: 162°; 20; 5x + 100 = 540 so x = 88. extend: for n > 4 exterior = 360/n < 90 since n > 4. stretch: exterior e and interior 5e: 6e = 180 so e = 30, n = 12.

practice: Find the angle sum of a 12-sided polygon.
A regular octagon: find an exterior angle and an interior angle.
Hexagon angles: 130°, 115°, 140°, 125°, 100° and x. Find x.
A regular polygon has interior angle 162°. How many sides has it?
independent: Core: a) Interior angle of a regular 20-gon. b) Number of sides if the exterior angle is 18°. c) Pentagon angles x, x + 10, x + 20, x + 30 and x + 40: find x.
Extend: Show that the exterior angle of a regular polygon is always less than 90° for polygons with more than 4 sides.
Stretch: The interior angle of a regular polygon is five times the exterior. Find the number of sides.
exit: Find the sum of the interior angles of a heptagon.
A regular polygon has exterior angle 45°. How many sides?
Big question: Is there a rule that works for every polygon?
lessons.homework: Explain in words why the exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360° (think of walking round it, turning at each corner).
lessons.send: SEND: use cut-out triangles to build the polygon sum. EAL: 'interior', 'exterior', 'regular'. Stretch: angle sum in non-convex polygons and spiral proof.

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Ruler and compass constructions
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we draw perfectly accurate shapes using only a ruler and compasses?
objectives: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line
Construct an angle bisector and a perpendicular from a point
Construct a triangle given three sides and a 60° angle
successCriteria: All: follow a construction method accurately and leave the arcs visible
Most: construct triangles from SSS and a 60° angle
Some: explain why a construction works
lessons.smsc: Geometric constructions are at the heart of Islamic patterns: precision and patience produce beauty.

keywords.def: draw accurately with a ruler and compasses, leaving the construction arcs
part of a circle
a line that cuts something exactly in half

starter: Bismillah. What is the size of each angle in an equilateral triangle?
Draw a chord and a radius of a circle (describe it) and name the longest chord.

teach.heading: Perpendicular bisector of AB
cycle: Open the compasses to more than half of AB
Put the point on A and draw an arc above and below AB
Keep the same width; put the point on B and draw crossing arcs
Join the two crossing points with a ruler
This line cuts AB in half at 90°
teach.note: Demonstrate live with GeoGebra or on paper under the camera. Pupils need paper, compasses and a ruler, ideally pencil. Stress: do NOT rub out the arcs, since they show the method and earn the marks.
bullets: Same compass width for both arcs

teach.heading: Four key constructions

head: Construction
Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
rows: Arcs from A, radius over half AB
Arc from B cuts both arms at P and Q
Arcs of equal radius from P and Q
Join B to where the arcs cross
Perpendicular from point P to line
Arc from P cuts the line at X and Y
Equal arcs from X and Y
Join P to where arcs cross
Arc from A cuts the line at X
Arc of same radius from X crosses first arc at Y

teach.note: Go through each row with a quick demonstration. Ask which of these uses a fixed compass width throughout. Another approach: build each as a flowchart on the whiteboard.
bullets: Compasses fixed: leave arcs visible

teach.heading: Triangle from three sides (SSS)

model.problem: Construct triangle ABC with AB = 6 cm, BC = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm.
steps: Draw AB = 6 cm with a ruler
Compasses 4 cm, centre A: draw an arc
Compasses 5 cm, centre B: draw an arc crossing the first at C

teach.note: Check by measuring. Discuss why you cannot form a triangle from 2, 3 and 7 cm: the arcs do not cross (triangle inequality).

teach.heading: Hinge: perpendicular bisector

check.q: When constructing the perpendicular bisector of AB, the compass radius must be:
options: any size, but different for A and B
check.why: Arcs must cross, so the radius must exceed half of AB. The same radius is used from A and B. Using less than half gives arcs that do not meet.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask 'what happens with a radius of exactly half?' (arcs touch at the midpoint only).

teach.heading: Why it works (Higher)
bullets: The arcs make a rhombus with all four sides equal
A rhombus has diagonals that bisect at right angles
So every point on the bisector is equal distance from A and B
Triangles formed are congruent by SSS
teach.note: Link to G6: show with diagram words: A and B joined to both crossing points give four equal sides. Ask why the line must pass through the midpoint (diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other). ANSWERS: practice: arcs of more than 4.5 cm from each end; triangle drawn; 35° each; angles 60°. exit: arcs must be visible as evidence of the method; 3-4-5 is a right-angled triangle (90° between 3 and 4). core: PR is about 7.2 cm by measuring (7.21 by calculation). extend: arc from P cuts line at X and Y; equal arcs from X and Y cross below the line; join. stretch: bisect the 60° to get 30°; construct perpendicular bisector of the line for 90°. homework: rhombus of side 5 with 60°: a diagonal splits it into two equilateral triangles.

practice: Describe how to construct the perpendicular bisector of a 9 cm line.
Construct a triangle with sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.
Draw an angle of 70° using a protractor and bisect it. What is the size of each part?
Construct an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm and state its angles.
independent: Core: a) Construct a triangle PQR with PQ = 8 cm, QR = 6 cm and angle PQR = 60° (construct the 60°). b) Measure PR.
Extend: Construct the perpendicular from point P to a line AB, where P is 4 cm above the line.
Stretch: Construct a 30° angle and a 90° angle from your 60° construction. Explain how.
exit: Why must the arcs be left on the paper?
Construct a triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. What angle do you notice?
Big question: How do we draw perfectly accurate shapes using only a ruler and compasses?
lessons.homework: Construct a rhombus with sides 5 cm and an angle of 60° using only compasses and a ruler. Then draw one diagonal and say what you notice.
lessons.send: SEND: provide pre-drawn lines with marked start points; use a larger compass if needed. EAL: pre-teach 'arc', 'bisector', 'compasses'. Stretch: construct a 15° or 75° angle. Higher-only: explaining why constructions work.

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Loci
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a rule describe a region on a map?
objectives: Describe and draw the four standard loci
Combine loci to find a region
Test whether a point is in a region
successCriteria: All: draw loci for fixed distance from a point and a line
Most: draw loci equidistant from two points or lines
Some: combine several rules and shade the correct region
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and technology: signal range, safe zones, fences
lessons.smsc: Safety and care for others (amanah): keeping safe distances and defining space respectfully.

keywords.def: the set of all points that obey a rule
the same distance from two things
an area of points satisfying one or more rules

starter: Construct (describe) the perpendicular bisector of AB.
Describe how to bisect an angle.

teach.heading: The four basic loci

head: Rule
Locus
Construction
rows: Fixed distance from a line segment
Two parallel lines with semicircles at the ends (a 'racetrack')
Equidistant from two points A and B
Angle bisector (of the angle between them)

teach.note: Pupils copy this table; it organises every loci question. Ask: which two are lines? Which is a curve? Stress 'nearer to A than B' means the region on A's side of the bisector.
bullets: Closer to means one side of the locus

teach.heading: Hinge: racetrack

check.q: Which describes all points exactly 3 cm from a straight line segment AB of length 8 cm?
options: A 'racetrack': two parallel lines 3 cm away joined by semicircles at A and B
check.why: Points near the ends are 3 cm from A or B, giving semicircles. Two lines alone miss the ends.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Draw the shape in the air or under the camera.

teach.heading: Combining loci

model.problem: Rectangle ABCD has A(0, 0), B(8, 0), C(8, 6), D(0, 6), lengths in metres. Treasure is closer to A than to B, closer to AB than to AD, and within 5 m of C. Is the point R(3.9, 3.5) in the region?
steps: Closer to A than B: x < 4. 3.9 < 4 ✓
Closer to AB than AD: y < x. 3.5 < 3.9 ✓

teach.note: On paper the bisector of AB is x = 4 and the bisector of angle DAB is the line y = x. Test one boundary point to decide which side to shade. Check: P(3, 2) fails because its distance to C is √41 ≈ 6.4 m.

teach.heading: Boundaries and shading

misconception.wrong: Draw the locus lines and shade anywhere near them.
misconception.right: Decide the side of each line from the wording, shade only the overlap, and use a dashed line if the boundary is excluded.

teach.note: Ask: for 'closer to A than to B', which side of the bisector holds A? Test with the point A itself. Use 'less than' for inside the circle.

teach.heading: Using a locus in context
bullets: A router reaches 12 m: points within 12 m form a circle
A path must be 2 m from a wall: a parallel line
A new bench is equal distance from two paths: an angle bisector
Scale: 1 cm to 2 m, convert before drawing
teach.note: Pick a context from the pupils' world: a masjid car park, a school field. Always work out the scale before drawing and state whether to use a ruler/compasses (construct) or measure. ANSWERS: practice: circle of radius 5 m centred on T; the line through the midpoint of PQ, parallel to QR (5 cm from P and Q); (2, 1) satisfies both rules since x < 3 and its distance from O is √5 ≈ 2.2 < 4; a racetrack 2 cm either side with semicircles at the ends. exit: the angle bisector(s); a circle of radius 4 cm. extend: the sprinkler is at one point, 3 m above AB and about 3.3 m from AD (on the plan 1.5 cm above AB and 1.66 cm from AD). stretch: a lens-shaped overlap of two circles of radius 20 km. core: check by measuring.

practice: A tree stands at T. Describe the locus of points within 5 m of T.
Rectangle PQRS has PQ = 10 cm and QR = 6 cm. Describe the locus of points equidistant from P and Q.
Test (2, 1) against 'closer to O(0, 0) than to B(6, 0)' and 'within 4 units of O'.
Draw the locus of points 2 cm from a 5 cm line.
independent: Core: a) Triangle ABC with AB = 8 cm, BC = 7 cm, AC = 6 cm (construct it). Shade the region closer to A than to B and within 5 cm of C. b) A point is equidistant from AB and AC and 4 cm from A: mark it.
Extend: A garden is rectangle 12 m by 8 m, scale 1 cm : 2 m. A sprinkler is 3 m from side AB and 6 m from corner D. Show where it can be.
Stretch: A radio mast sends a signal 20 km. Two masts are 30 km apart. Show the area covered by both.
exit: Describe the locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines.
Describe the locus of points exactly 4 cm from a point P.
Big question: How can a rule describe a region on a map?
lessons.homework: Design a safe zone for a school sports day: describe it as a combination of two loci and draw it for a 20 m by 30 m field.
lessons.send: SEND: give each locus rule on a card and pre-drawn diagrams; shade with colour. EAL: 'equidistant', 'locus', 'region'. Stretch: loci in 3D (a point 5 cm from a plane: two parallel planes).

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Congruence and simple proofs
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know two triangles are exactly the same without measuring everything?
objectives: State and use the congruence criteria SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS and RHS
Explain why AAA and SSA are not enough
Write a short proof using congruent triangles
successCriteria: All: decide whether two triangles are congruent and give the criterion
Most: use congruent triangles to find a missing length or angle
Some: write a proof with statement and reason
lessons.smsc: Accuracy and honesty in argument: a proof states every reason.

keywords.def: identical in shape and size
the angle between two given sides
a logical argument showing a statement is always true

starter: State the angle sum of a triangle.
Find the missing angle in a triangle with 48° and 75°.
Name the property of an isosceles triangle's base angles.

teach.heading: Congruence criteria

head: Criterion
What matches
Example
rows: two sides and the angle between them

teach.note: Show each with triangles drawn in words. Stress that AAA gives similar, not congruent. SSA can fail: two different triangles are possible. Link back to constructions: SSS and SAS are constructions you can do.
bullets: Always say which criterion

teach.heading: A proof

model.problem: ABCD is a kite with AB = AD and CB = CD. Prove triangles ABC and ADC are congruent, and hence that angle ABC = angle ADC.
steps: AC is common to both triangles
So triangles ABC and ADC are congruent (SSS)
Hence angle ABC = angle ADC (corresponding angles of congruent triangles)

teach.note: Format: statement then reason. Insist on 'congruent (SSS)' and the final 'corresponding angles'. Ask pupils to keep the vertices in matching order.

teach.heading: Hinge: SSA

check.q: Triangle 1 has sides 5 cm and 6 cm and a 40° angle which is NOT between them. Triangle 2 has the same. Must they be congruent?
options: No: the angle is not included, so they may differ
check.why: The congruence rule needs the included angle (SAS). With a non-included angle, two different triangles can be made. AAA shows similarity only.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Show why: swing the 5 cm side from the end of the 6 cm side to cut the base line in two places.

teach.heading: Isosceles triangle proof

model.problem: In triangle PQR, PQ = PR. S is the midpoint of QR. Prove angle PQR = angle PRQ.
steps: Triangles PQS and PRS are congruent (SSS)
So angle PQS = angle PRS: base angles of isosceles triangle are equal

teach.note: This justifies a fact pupils have used since KS3. Ask: what other criterion could we use if PS were perpendicular to QR? (RHS).

teach.heading: Matching vertices

misconception.wrong: Triangle ABC is congruent to PQR because they have 3 equal angles.
misconception.right: They are congruent if SSS, SAS, ASA or RHS holds; equal angles give similarity only.

teach.note: Show two equilateral triangles of side 2 and 5: same angles but different sizes. ANSWERS: practice: SSS; SAS; ASA; RHS; AB = DC (opposite sides), BC common, angle ABC = angle DCB = 90° so SAS; No: only similar; AM common, BM = CM, right angles so SAS so AB = AC. exit: SSA; sides and common side so SSS. extend: PQ = PS, QR = SR, PR common so SSS so angle QPR = angle SPR. stretch: triangles BDC and CEB: BC common, angle B = angle C, BD = CE so SAS, so BE = CD.

practice: State which criterion proves congruence: (a) 5, 7, 9 and 9, 5, 7; (b) 6, 8, 50° between and the same; (c) 40°, 60°, 7 cm between and the same; (d) right angle, hypotenuse 13, side 5 and the same.
ABCD is a rectangle. Prove that triangles ABC and DCB are congruent.
Two triangles have angles 50°, 60°, 70°. Are they congruent? Explain.
In triangle ABC, M is the midpoint of BC, and AM is perpendicular to BC. Prove AB = AC.
independent: Core: a) Prove the diagonals of a rectangle are equal. b) In a parallelogram ABCD, prove AB = CD from triangles ABC and CDA by showing they are congruent (use alternate angles).
Extend: PQRS is a kite. Prove PR bisects angle QPS.
Stretch: Triangle ABC with AB = AC; D on AB and E on AC with BD = CE. Prove BE = CD.
exit: Which criterion is not a congruence criterion: SAS, SSA, ASA, SSS?
Write one reason for each step of: AB = AD, BC = DC, AC common, so ABC and ADC are congruent.
Big question: How do we know two triangles are exactly the same without measuring everything?
lessons.homework: Prove the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other by finding two congruent triangles. Name the criterion.
lessons.send: SEND: give a proof frame with the statements and the reason bank. EAL: sentence stems 'so triangles ... are congruent (...)'. Stretch: show a counter-example for SSA with a diagram. Higher-only: formal proofs with reasons (G6).

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Enlargements with positive, fractional and negative scale factors
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to a shape when the scale factor is negative?
objectives: Enlarge a shape with a positive or fractional scale factor from a given centre
Enlarge with a negative scale factor
Describe an enlargement fully and say which transformations give congruent or similar images
successCriteria: All: enlarge on a grid from the origin with a positive scale factor
Most: enlarge with a fractional or negative scale factor and a given centre
Some: find the centre and scale factor of an enlargement
lessons.smsc: Proportion in Islamic art: patterns that keep their shape as they grow.

keywords.def: a transformation that changes size from a centre by a scale factor
the fixed point from which a shape is enlarged
how many times larger or smaller the image is

starter: A rectangle is 3 cm by 5 cm. Enlarge by scale factor 4: find the new sides.
Find the area of the enlarged rectangle as a multiple of the original.

teach.heading: Enlarging a triangle from the origin
teach.note: Each coordinate is multiplied by the scale factor when the centre is the origin. Ask: where is the negative image relative to the object? (the other side of the centre, upside down, a rotation of 180° followed by enlargement).
bullets: Multiply coordinates by the scale factor
Negative: opposite side of the centre

teach.heading: Centre not at the origin

model.problem: Enlarge triangle A(2, 1), B(5, 1), C(2, 3) by scale factor -2 with centre (1, 0).
steps: Vector from centre to A is (1, 1); × -2 gives (-2, -2); add centre: A' = (-1, -2)

teach.note: Method: vector from the centre to the point, multiply it, then add the centre back. The image is twice as big, inverted, on the opposite side.

teach.heading: Hinge: negative scale factor

check.q: A shape is enlarged by scale factor -3. The image is:
options: 3 times as big, on the same side of the centre
3 times as big, on the opposite side, and turned upside down
one third the size, on the opposite side
3 times as big and reflected in a line through the centre
check.why: Negative scale factor: the image is on the opposite side of the centre and rotated 180°. Its size is the modulus of the scale factor.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the area factor (9).

teach.heading: Finding the centre

model.problem: Under an enlargement the point (2, 2) maps to (4, 4) and the point (3, 2) maps to (7, 4). Find the centre and the scale factor.
steps: Line through (3, 2) and (7, 4): gradient 1/2 so y = x/2 + 1/2
Lines meet when x = x/2 + 1/2 so x = 1: centre (1, 1)
Scale factor: (7, 4) - (1, 1) = (6, 3) which is 3 × (2, 1), so sf 3

teach.note: On a grid draw rays through corresponding points: they meet at the centre. Describe fully: 'enlargement', scale factor, centre. All three needed for full marks.

teach.heading: Which transformations?
teach.note: Close with the structure of G7: congruent shapes keep size, similar shapes keep angle and ratio of sides. Ask a pupil to give an example of each. ANSWERS: practice: (3, 3), (12, 3), (3, 9); (0.5, 0.5), (2, 0.5), (0.5, 1.5); (0, 0), (-2, 0), (-2, -2), (0, -2); enlargement, scale factor 1/2, centre O. exit: (-4, -6); 1/4. core: (1.5, 1.5), (6.5, 1.5), (1.5, 4); area scale factor 6.25. extend: enlargement, scale factor -1, centre O. stretch: area factor 9 so scale factor 3 and the side is 12 cm. homework: both send each point P to the point the same distance from the centre on the opposite side.

practice: Enlarge the triangle (1, 1), (4, 1), (1, 3) by sf 3, centre O.
Enlarge the same triangle by sf 1/2 from centre O.
Enlarge the square (2, 2), (4, 2), (4, 4), (2, 4) by sf -1 with centre (1, 1).
Describe the transformation: (4, 2), (8, 2), (4, 6) maps to (2, 1), (4, 1), (2, 3).
independent: Core: a) Enlarge the triangle (0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1) by sf 2.5 from centre (-1, -1). b) Find the area scale factor.
Extend: The triangle A(1, 1), B(3, 1), C(1, 2) is mapped to A'(-1, -1), B'(-3, -1), C'(-1, -2). Describe the transformation fully.
Stretch: Triangle T has area 6 cm². An enlargement of T has area 54 cm². Find the scale factor and, if one side of T is 4 cm, the length of the corresponding side.
exit: Enlarge (2, 3) by sf -2, centre O.
State the scale factor of an enlargement that maps a side 12 cm to 3 cm.
Big question: What happens to a shape when the scale factor is negative?
lessons.homework: Explain why an enlargement with scale factor -1 is the same as a rotation of 180° about the same centre.
lessons.send: SEND: use coordinate grids with drawn rays and a vector method. EAL: 'enlargement', 'scale factor', 'centre'. Stretch: enlarge a circle; prove the image of a line is parallel to the original. Higher-only: negative scale factors (Foundation: positive and fractional).

lessons.unit: G1-G8: Geometry and measures: properties, constructions and transformations
lessons.title: Combining transformations
lessons.bigQuestion: If we reflect twice, is the result always a reflection?
objectives: Combine reflections, rotations and translations
Describe the single transformation equivalent to two reflections
Recognise that the order of transformations matters
successCriteria: All: apply two transformations in order
Most: describe two reflections as a translation or a rotation
Some: find the centre and angle of a combined rotation and translation
lessons.crossCurricular: Pattern making: repeated glides and rotations
lessons.smsc: Symmetry and pattern in Islamic tilings built from repeated reflections and rotations.

keywords.def: applying one transformation after another
a point that does not move
the line a shape is reflected in

teach.heading: Two reflections

head: First mirror
Second mirror
Equivalent single transformation
rows: Translation 6 right (twice the distance between mirrors, 2 × 3)
Rotation 180° about O (twice the 90° angle between mirrors)

teach.note: Walk through each row with a point such as (2, 1). Rule: parallel mirrors give a translation perpendicular to them of twice the distance. Intersecting mirrors give a rotation about the intersection of twice the angle between them. Order changes the direction.
bullets: Order matters

teach.heading: Rotation then translation

model.problem: Triangle with A(1, 1), B(3, 1), C(1, 2) is rotated 90° anticlockwise about O then translated by (3, -1). Find the image and a single equivalent transformation.
steps: Fixed point: x = -y + 3 and y = x - 1 so x = 2, y = 1
model.answer: A'(2, 0), B'(2, 2), C'(1, 0); rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1)

teach.note: Check A: vector from (2, 1) to A is (-1, 0); rotating 90° anticlockwise gives (0, -1) so A' = (2, 0). The mix of a rotation and translation is another rotation of the same angle.

teach.heading: Hinge: two parallel mirrors

check.q: A shape is reflected in x = 2 and then in x = 5. The single equivalent transformation is:
check.why: Twice the distance between the mirrors: 2 × 3 = 6 to the right. 3 is only the distance between mirrors; reflection in x = 3.5 is a single mirror line.

teach.note: Test with (0, 1): x = 4 - 0 = 4 after first, then 10 - 4 = 6 after second: moved 6.

teach.heading: Order of transformations

misconception.wrong: Rotation then reflection is the same as reflection then rotation.
misconception.right: In general the order matters: the images can be in different positions.

teach.note: Use the triangle with vertex (2, 1): rotate 90° about O then reflect in the x-axis gives (-1, -2); reflect in the x-axis then rotate gives (1, 2). Different results.

teach.heading: What stays the same?
bullets: Reflections, rotations and translations keep size and shape
So any combination gives a congruent image
Enlargement changes size, so the image is similar
Always give the order when you describe a combination
teach.note: Check G7: in 'congruent or similar', the key test is whether lengths change. Ask pupils to say whether a combination of an enlargement and reflection is congruent (no). ANSWERS: practice: (-1, 2), rotation 90° anticlockwise about O; translation 10 right; (-3, 4); reflection in the x-axis. exit: 14 right; no. core: translation 8 right; reflection in the y-axis. extend: rotation 90° clockwise sends (x, y) to (y, -x); images A'(-1, -1), B'(-1, -3), C'(-2, -1). stretch: rotation 90° anticlockwise about (2, 1). homework: 6 cm.

practice: Reflect (2, 1) in y = 0 then in y = x. State the final point and the single transformation.
Reflect in x = 1 then x = 6: describe the single transformation.
Translate by (2, 3) then by (-5, 1): find the single translation.
Reflect in the y-axis then rotate 180° about O: describe the single transformation.
independent: Core: a) Rotation 180° about O then 180° about (4, 0). b) Reflect in y = 0, then x = 0, then y = 0: what single transformation?
Extend: Triangle (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2): rotate 90° clockwise about O then reflect in the y-axis. Find the image.
Stretch: Describe fully a rotation 90° anticlockwise about O followed by a translation (3, -1) that is equivalent to a single rotation, and find its centre.
exit: Reflect in x = 3 then in x = 10: find the translation.
State whether a rotation then reflection is always the same as reflection then rotation.
Big question: If we reflect twice, is the result always a reflection?
lessons.homework: A pattern is made by reflecting a tile in a mirror, then reflecting the result in a second parallel mirror 3 cm away. How far has the tile moved overall?
lessons.send: SEND: use tracing paper and coordinate grids. EAL: 'followed by', 'equivalent', 'mirror'. Stretch: show that two rotations about different centres give a translation when the angles add to 360°. Higher-only: describing a combination as a single transformation (G8).

lessons.unit: G15-G19: Geometry and measures: measuring, mensuration and similarity
lessons.title: Measuring, bearings and scale drawings
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we describe a direction using just three digits?
objectives: Measure lines and angles accurately
Write and use three-figure bearings
Find a back bearing and use scale drawings to solve bearing problems
successCriteria: All: measure and draw a bearing
Most: find the bearing of A from B given the bearing of B from A
Some: solve a two-leg journey by scale drawing and reasoning
lessons.smsc: Direction in worship: the qibla is found by a bearing, and Muslims through history used maps, instruments and angle measurement to find it.

keywords.def: an angle measured clockwise from north, written with three figures
the bearing of the return journey
an instrument for measuring angles

starter: Angles on a straight line add to what?
Alternate angles between parallel lines are what?

teach.heading: Three rules for bearings
bullets: Measure from north
Measure clockwise
Always give three figures: 5° is 005°
Draw a north line at the starting point
