teach.note: Pupils draw a compass rose in their books. Insist on the north line before measuring. Common error: measuring anticlockwise or from the wrong point. The bearing 'of B from A' means standing at A, looking at B.

teach.heading: Back bearings

model.problem: The bearing of B from A is 065°. Find the bearing of A from B.
steps: Draw north lines at A and B: they are parallel
At A, line AB makes 65° with north
By alternate angles, the angle at B between BA and the south direction is 65°
So the bearing of A from B = 180° + 65° = 245°

teach.note: Rule: add 180° if the bearing is under 180°, subtract 180° if it is over 180°. Show with a sketch: two parallel north lines and alternate angles.

teach.heading: Hinge: back bearing

check.q: The bearing of A from B is 120°. What is the bearing of B from A?
check.why: 120° + 180° = 300°. 060 is 180 - 120; 240 is 360 - 120 which is a reflection error; 120 ignores the change of point.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for a sketch.

teach.heading: Scale drawing

model.problem: A hiker walks 5 km on a bearing of 040° and then 4 km on 130°. Find how far from the start she is, and the bearing of the finish from the start.
steps: Scale 1 cm : 1 km. Draw 5 cm at 040° from north, then 4 cm at 130° from a north line at the end
The turn is 130° - 40° = 90°, so right-angled: distance √(5² + 4²) = √41 ≈ 6.4 km

teach.note: Accept 6.4 ± 0.1 km and 079° ± 2° from a scale drawing. Check the measured answer with the Pythagoras method as a cross-check. Trigonometry is covered in Year 11.

teach.heading: Measuring and accuracy
bullets: Measure lines to the nearest millimetre
Measure angles to the nearest degree
State the scale and the units
Estimate before you measure: is the answer sensible?
teach.note: Practise with a protractor: align the base line and the centre, read the right scale. Ask how much error is acceptable in an exam (usually 2° and 2 mm). ANSWERS: practice: 252°; 005° and about north-west (55° west of north); AB = 7.5 cm on the drawing = 15 km (9² + 12² = 15²); 13 km. exit: 007° and 035°. core: 105°; south-east. extend: Z is 6.93 km east and 6 km north of Y, so YZ = √84 ≈ 9.2 km. stretch: angle at A = 90° - 50° = 40° and angle at B = 320° - 270° = 50°, so angle C = 180° - 90° = 90°. homework: 299° (a rough straight-line bearing only; the true great-circle return bearing differs).

practice: The bearing of Q from P is 072°. Find the bearing of P from Q.
Write the bearing 5° as a three-figure bearing, and 305° as a direction in words.
A lighthouse L. Ship A is 9 km away on 130° and ship B is 12 km on 220°. Draw at scale 1 cm : 2 km and measure AB. Check by Pythagoras.

objectives: Use area formulae for triangles, parallelograms and trapezia
Find the volume and surface area of prisms including cylinders

successCriteria: All: find areas of triangles, parallelograms and trapezia

keywords.def: the height at right angles to the base
the shape you see when you cut straight through a prism
a solid with the same cross-section all along its length

starter: Work out the area of a rectangle 9 cm by 4.5 cm.

teach.heading: Area and volume formulae
teach.note: Triangle, parallelogram and trapezium formulae must be recalled; they are not given in the exam. Show a trapezium made from two triangles, or two copies of the trapezium forming a parallelogram of base (a + b).
bullets: Use perpendicular height, not the slant side

teach.heading: Trapezium

model.problem: A trapezium has parallel sides 8 cm and 14 cm, 5 cm apart. Find its area.

teach.note: Two copies make a parallelogram with base 22 cm and height 5 cm: 110 cm², so one is 55 cm².

teach.heading: Hinge: parallelogram

check.q: A parallelogram has base 9 cm, slanted side 6 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. Its area is:
check.why: Area = base × perpendicular height = 9 × 5 = 45. 54 uses the slant side; 27 halves it as if it were a triangle.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask why the slant side is irrelevant: rectangle with a triangle moved from one end to the other.

teach.heading: Prism and cylinder

model.problem: A triangular prism has base 6 cm, height 4 cm and length 10 cm. A cylinder has radius 3.5 cm and height 12 cm. Find both volumes.

teach.note: Link: every prism uses 'area of the cross-section × length'. Give the answer to 3 s.f. or in terms of π: 147π cm³. 1 cm³ = 1 ml so the cylinder holds about 0.46 litres.

teach.heading: Surface area of a cylinder

misconception.right: Total surface area = 2πrh + 2πr² (curved surface plus two circles)

teach.note: Net: a rectangle of width 2πr and height h plus two circles. Ask pupils to decide whether the question wants the curved surface only or the total. ANSWERS: practice: 32 cm²; 58.5 cm²; 360 cm³; V = 160π ≈ 502.7 cm³, total SA = 80π + 32π = 112π ≈ 351.9 cm². exit: 90 cm²; 200π ≈ 628.3 cm³. core: 90 cm²; 48 cm²; cross-section 28 cm², volume 336 cm³. extend: h = 500 ÷ (16π) ≈ 9.95 cm. stretch: 36π × 20 = 720π ≈ 2261.9 cm³ then ÷ 600 ≈ 3.77 cm. homework: V = π × 3.5² × 11 = 134.75π ≈ 423.3 ml; label = 2π × 3.5 × 11 = 77π ≈ 241.9 cm².

practice: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm. Find its area.
A triangle has base 13 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. Find its area.
A triangular prism has cross-section area 24 cm² and length 15 cm. Find its volume.
A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 10 cm. Find its volume and total surface area, in terms of π.
independent: Core: a) Parallelogram base 12 cm, perpendicular height 7.5 cm: area. b) A rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm with a rectangle 4 cm by 3 cm cut out: area. c) A prism with trapezium cross-section (parallel sides 5 cm and 9 cm, height 4 cm) and length 12 cm: volume.
Extend: A cylinder has volume 500 cm³ and radius 4 cm. Find its height to 3 s.f.
Stretch: Water in a cylinder of radius 6 cm and height 20 cm is poured into a rectangular tank with base 30 cm by 20 cm. Find the rise in water level.
exit: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 12 cm and height 7.5 cm.

lessons.homework: A can has radius 3.5 cm and height 11 cm. Find the volume in ml and the area of paper needed for the label, which covers only the curved surface.
lessons.send: SEND: use cut-out shapes to show triangle and trapezium areas; supply the formulae card. EAL: 'perpendicular', 'cross-section'. Stretch: derive the trapezium formula.

lessons.title: Circles: circumference, area and composite shapes
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does the number π appear in every circle?
objectives: Use the circumference and area formulae of a circle
Give answers in terms of π
Find perimeter and area of semicircles and composite shapes
successCriteria: All: find circumference and area from a radius or diameter

keywords.def: the distance round a circle
a chord through the centre; twice the radius
the ratio circumference ÷ diameter, about 3.14159

starter: Write down the area of a rectangle 12 m by 7.5 m.
Rearrange C = πd to make d the subject.

teach.heading: Two formulae
bullets: Circumference C = πd = 2πr
Area A = πr²
An exact answer is left in terms of π
Use the π button, not 3.14, for decimals
teach.note: Both formulae must be recalled. Highlight: radius is half the diameter and the order: square the radius first and then multiply by π. Typical error: (πr)² or using diameter in the area formula.

teach.heading: Working backwards

model.problem: The area of a circle is 100 cm². Find its radius to 3 s.f.

teach.note: Reverse operations: divide by π then take the square root. Link to C = 30 cm: r = 30 ÷ (2π) = 4.77 cm.

teach.heading: Composite perimeter

model.problem: A running track has two straights of 40 m and two semicircular ends of diameter 20 m. Find the perimeter and the area.
steps: Two semicircles make a circle of diameter 20 m: circumference 20π

teach.note: Combine the two semicircles as one circle. Compare with an answer in terms of π: 80 + 20π and 800 + 100π.

teach.heading: Hinge: circumference

check.q: A circle has diameter 10 cm. Its circumference is:
check.why: C = πd = 10π. 25π is the area (π × 5²); 5π comes from using r instead of d; 100π squares the diameter.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask which option is the area (25π).

teach.heading: Window shape

model.problem: A window is a rectangle 80 cm wide and 120 cm high with a semicircle of diameter 80 cm on top. Find the area and the perimeter.

teach.note: The base of the semicircle is not part of the perimeter, as it is inside the shape. ANSWERS: practice: 14π ≈ 44.0 cm; 49π ≈ 153.9 cm²; area 12.5π ≈ 39.3 cm², perimeter 5π + 10 ≈ 25.7 cm; r ≈ 4.77 cm. exit: 36π; 28.3 cm. core: r = 10 so 100π cm²; rectangle 12 × 8 = 96 plus a circle of diameter 8: 16π, total 96 + 16π ≈ 146.3 cm². extend: 100 - 25π ≈ 21.5 cm². stretch: π × 4² - π × 3² = 7π ≈ 22.0 m². homework: 1.44π ≈ 4.52 m² and about £135.72.

practice: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 14 cm.
Find the area of a circle with radius 7 cm, in terms of π and to 1 d.p.
A semicircle has diameter 10 cm. Find its area and perimeter.
A circle has circumference 30 cm. Find its radius.
independent: Core: a) A circle has circumference 20π cm: find its area in terms of π. b) Find the area of a shape made from a rectangle 12 cm by 8 cm with a semicircle of diameter 8 cm on each short end.
Extend: Find the area of a square of side 10 cm with a circle of the largest possible size cut out.
Stretch: A circular pond of radius 3 m has a path 1 m wide round it. Find the area of the path.
exit: Find the area of a circle with radius 6 cm in terms of π.
Find the circumference of a circle of diameter 9 cm to 1 d.p.
Big question: Why does the number π appear in every circle?
lessons.homework: A circular rug has diameter 2.4 m. Find its area, and the cost at £30 per square metre.
lessons.send: SEND: label every diagram with r and d and use a two-column π and decimal answer. EAL: 'circumference', 'diameter', 'radius'. Stretch: perimeter and area of the shaded region between two circles.

lessons.unit: G15-G19: Geometry and measures: measuring, mensuration and similarity
lessons.title: Spheres and cones
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is a sphere's volume exactly two thirds of its tight-fitting cylinder?
objectives: Use the volume and surface area formulae for spheres
Use the volume and curved surface area of a cone
Work with hemispheres and rearrange to find a radius
successCriteria: All: calculate the volume and surface area of a sphere
Most: calculate cone volume, curved and total surface area using slant height
Some: solve problems involving hemispheres, melting and solving for radius

keywords.def: a perfectly round solid
half a sphere
the length of the sloping side of a cone

starter: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 2 cm and height 5 cm in terms of π.
Use Pythagoras: a right-angled triangle has sides 5 and 12. Find the hypotenuse.

teach.heading: Formulae for sphere and cone
teach.note: The first four formulae are given in the exam question; the rest must be built from them. l is the slant height; h is the perpendicular height. They are related by l² = r² + h². Ask which pupils would be unsure which of l and h to use.
bullets: l² = r² + h²

teach.heading: Sphere

model.problem: A sphere has radius 6 cm. Find its volume and surface area.

teach.note: Leave answers in terms of π first: 288π cm³ and 144π cm². Cube the radius, not the diameter.

teach.heading: Cone

model.problem: A cone has radius 5 cm and perpendicular height 12 cm. Find its volume, curved surface area and total surface area.

teach.note: Use h in the volume and l in the curved surface. Show a sector net of the curved surface.

teach.heading: Hinge: hemisphere

check.q: The volume of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm is:
check.why: A sphere of radius 3 has V = 4/3 π × 27 = 36π. Half of this is 18π. 36π is the whole sphere; 54π is 2π r³ applied wrongly.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the total surface area of this hemisphere (27π cm²).

teach.heading: Mixing up h and l

misconception.right: Volume uses the perpendicular height h; curved surface area uses the slant height l

teach.note: For r = 5, h = 12: V uses 12, curved SA uses 13. ANSWERS: practice: 288π ≈ 905 cm³ and 144π ≈ 452 cm²; 100π ≈ 314 cm³ and 65π ≈ 204 cm²; V = 18π ≈ 56.5 cm³ and total SA = 27π ≈ 84.8 cm²; r = 3 cm. exit: V = 256π/3 ≈ 268 cm³ and SA = 64π ≈ 201 cm²; 15π ≈ 47.1 cm². core: l = 10, V = 96π ≈ 301.6, SA = 60π + 36π = 96π ≈ 301.6; r = 5 cm and V = 500π/3 ≈ 523.6 cm³. extend: 27 spheres. stretch: 1/3 π r² h = 2/3 π r³ so h = 2r. homework: r = 11, V = 4/3 π × 1331 ≈ 5575 cm³ (5580 to 3 s.f.), SA = 4π × 121 = 484π ≈ 1520 cm².

practice: A sphere has radius 6 cm. Find its volume in terms of π and its surface area.
A cone has radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Find its volume and curved surface area.
Find the volume and total surface area of a hemisphere of radius 3 cm in terms of π.
A sphere has volume 36π cm³. Find its radius.
independent: Core: a) A cone has radius 6 cm and height 8 cm. Find the slant height, the volume and the total surface area. b) A sphere has surface area 100π cm². Find its radius and volume in terms of π.
Extend: A solid metal sphere of radius 9 cm is melted and made into small spheres of radius 3 cm. How many small spheres can be made?
Stretch: A cone and a hemisphere have the same radius r and equal volumes. Find the height of the cone in terms of r.
exit: Find the volume and surface area of a sphere of radius 4 cm in terms of π.
A cone has radius 3 cm and slant height 5 cm. Find its curved surface area in terms of π.
Big question: Why is a sphere's volume exactly two thirds of its tight-fitting cylinder?
lessons.homework: A football has diameter 22 cm. Find its volume in cm³ to 3 s.f. and the area of leather needed.
lessons.send: SEND: give the formula in a box and colour r, h, l on the diagram. EAL: 'sphere', 'hemisphere', 'slant'. Stretch: sphere and cone as limit cases; show cone volume is one third of cylinder. Higher-only: composite and reverse problems (the extend and stretch tasks).

lessons.unit: G15-G19: Geometry and measures: measuring, mensuration and similarity
lessons.title: Pyramids, frustums and composite solids
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we measure a solid made of several shapes?
objectives: Find the volume of a pyramid
Find the volume of a frustum by subtracting a cone
Solve problems with composite solids
successCriteria: All: calculate the volume of a pyramid
Most: calculate volume of composite solids made from cones, hemispheres and cylinders
Some: calculate a frustum volume using similar cones

keywords.def: a solid with a polygon base and triangular faces meeting at an apex
a cone or pyramid with the top removed
a solid made from simpler solids joined together

starter: Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 cm and height 4 cm in terms of π.
Find the area of a square base of side 8 cm.
A cone of height 6 cm is similar to a cone of height 12 cm. Find the scale factor.

teach.heading: Pyramid volume
bullets: V = 1/3 × area of base × perpendicular height
This formula is not given in the exam
Height is measured from the apex to the base at 90°
The slant height is a different length
teach.note: Show three pyramids filling a cube or prism, if possible with a physical model. Ask: how many pyramids fit in a prism of the same base and height? (three).

teach.heading: Pyramid

model.problem: A square-based pyramid has base side 8 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. Find its volume.

teach.note: Divide by 3. Common error: forgetting the factor of 1/3. Ask for the volume of the matching prism (576 cm³) as a check.

teach.heading: Composite solid

model.problem: An ice-cream is a cone of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm with a hemisphere of radius 3 cm on top. Find the total volume.

teach.note: Key: split the solid, find each volume, then add. Stress radius equals 3 for both. Leave in terms of π until the end.

teach.heading: Frustum

model.problem: A cone of radius 6 cm and height 12 cm has a small cone of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm removed from the top. Find the volume of the frustum.

teach.note: The small cone is similar to the large one with scale factor 1/2: volume 1/8 of the large (144π ÷ 8 = 18π). Use this as the check. Higher tier.

teach.heading: Hinge: frustum

check.q: The frustum made by removing a cone of volume 18π from a cone of volume 144π has volume:
check.why: Subtract: 144π - 18π = 126π. 162π adds instead; 72π halves the large cone.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask why we subtract (the removed cone is part of the large one). ANSWERS: practice: 192 cm³; 70 cm³; 48π ≈ 150.8 cm³; 126π ≈ 395.8 cm³. exit: 60 cm³; 12π ≈ 37.7 cm³. core: 12 cm; 24π + 32π/3 = 104π/3 ≈ 108.9 cm³. extend: the full cone has height 45 cm (small cone height 30 cm from 8/12 = h/(h + 15)); volume = 2160π - 640π = 1520π ≈ 4775 cm³. stretch: half-diagonal = 5√2 so height = √(169 - 50) = √119 ≈ 10.9; V = 1/3 × 100 × 10.9 ≈ 363.6 cm³. homework: 72π + 12π = 84π ≈ 263.9 m³.

practice: A square-based pyramid has base side 8 cm and height 9 cm. Find its volume.
A rectangular pyramid has base 6 cm by 5 cm and height 7 cm. Find its volume.
An ice cream is a cone of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm with a hemisphere on top. Find the volume in terms of π.
A frustum is a large cone of radius 6 cm, height 12 cm minus a top cone of radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. Find its volume.
independent: Core: a) A square-based pyramid has volume 100 cm³ and base side 5 cm. Find its height. b) A capsule is a cylinder of radius 2 cm and length 6 cm with a hemisphere at each end: volume.
Extend: A bucket is a frustum with top radius 12 cm, bottom radius 8 cm and height 15 cm. Find how tall the full cone would be, and the volume of the bucket.
Stretch: A square-based pyramid has base side 10 cm and the edge from the apex to a corner has length 13 cm. Find its volume.
exit: A square pyramid has base side 6 cm and height 5 cm. Find its volume.
Find the volume of a cone with radius 3 cm and height 4 cm in terms of π.
Big question: How do we measure a solid made of several shapes?
lessons.homework: A silo is a cylinder of radius 3 m and height 8 m topped by a cone of height 4 m. Find the volume in terms of π and in m³ to 1 d.p.
lessons.send: SEND: draw each solid separately with its dimensions labelled; use physical objects. EAL: 'frustum', 'apex', 'composite'. Stretch: derive the pyramid formula with the three-pyramids-in-a-cube argument. Higher-only: frustums by subtracting similar cones.

lessons.unit: G15-G19: Geometry and measures: measuring, mensuration and similarity
lessons.title: Arc length and sector area
lessons.bigQuestion: How much of a circle is a slice, and how do we measure it?
objectives: Find arc length and sector area as fractions of a circle
Find the angle or radius from an arc length or area
Find the perimeter of a sector and the area of a segment
successCriteria: All: calculate arc length and sector area
Most: find an angle or radius from a given arc length or sector area
Some: find the perimeter of a sector and area of a segment
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and design: pie charts and fans
lessons.smsc: Fair division: dividing a circle into equal shares.

keywords.def: part of the circumference
a region bounded by two radii and an arc
the region between a chord and an arc

starter: Find the circumference of a circle of radius 9 cm in terms of π.
Find the area of a circle of radius 9 cm in terms of π.

teach.heading: A fraction of the circle
bullets: Fraction = angle ÷ 360
Arc length = angle/360 × 2πr
Sector area = angle/360 × πr²
Perimeter of a sector = arc + 2r
teach.note: Show a pizza cut into slices of 60° (a sixth). The arc is a sixth of the circumference; the sector a sixth of the area. Ask what fraction a 90° sector is (a quarter).

teach.heading: Arc and sector

model.problem: A sector has radius 9 cm and angle 140°. Find the arc length and the sector area.

teach.note: Simplify the fraction first so the arithmetic is exact. Show each in terms of π before approximating.

teach.heading: Finding the angle

model.problem: A sector has radius 12 cm and arc length 15 cm. Find the angle at the centre.

teach.note: Reverse the steps: the arc length as a fraction of the whole circumference gives the angle. Do not round early.

teach.heading: Hinge: area of a sector

check.q: A 90° sector has radius 4 cm. Its area is:
check.why: Quarter of π × 4² = 16π ÷ 4 = 4π. 16π is the full circle; 2π is the arc length.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for the arc length (2π).

teach.heading: Segment (Higher)

model.problem: A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 60°. Find the area of the segment cut off by the chord.
steps: Triangle is equilateral, side 6: area = 1/2 × 6 × 6 × sin 60° = 9√3 ≈ 15.59

teach.note: Segment = sector - triangle. The triangle area ½ab sin C is taught later in Year 11, so introduce it as a given for this example; we return to it later. ANSWERS: practice: 4π ≈ 12.6 cm; 20π ≈ 62.8 cm²; θ = 40π ÷ (144π) × 360 = 100°; r = 9 cm. exit: arc 4π ≈ 12.6 cm; area 24π ≈ 75.4 cm². core: arc 2π ≈ 6.28 cm and area 8π ≈ 25.1 cm²; perimeter 16 + 2π ≈ 22.3 cm. extend: arc = 30 - 20 = 10 cm so angle = 10 ÷ (20π) × 360 ≈ 57.3°. stretch: each slice is 72°, arc = 1/5 × 24π ≈ 15.08, perimeter = 24 + 15.08 ≈ 39.1 cm. homework: 120° so arc = 1/3 × 18π = 6π ≈ 18.8 cm and area = 1/3 × 81π = 27π ≈ 84.8 cm².

practice: Find the arc length of a sector with radius 10 cm and angle 72°.
Find the sector area for the same sector.
A sector with radius 12 cm has area 40π cm². Find its angle.
A sector with angle 140° has arc length 7π cm. Find its radius.
independent: Core: a) A sector with radius 8 cm and angle 45°: arc length and area. b) Perimeter of that sector.
Extend: A sector has radius 10 cm and perimeter 30 cm. Find its angle to 1 d.p.
Stretch: A circular cake of radius 12 cm is cut into 5 equal sectors. Find the perimeter of each slice.
exit: Find the arc length and area of a sector with radius 12 cm and angle 60°.
State the formula for the perimeter of a sector.
Big question: How much of a circle is a slice, and how do we measure it?
lessons.homework: A minute hand of length 9 cm moves for 20 minutes. Find the length of the arc its tip travels and the area the hand sweeps.
lessons.send: SEND: use circles divided into fractions and fill in the 'fraction × whole' frame. EAL: 'sector', 'arc', 'chord'. Stretch: a segment area where the angle is not 60°. Higher-only: segment area (the final model and stretch task).

lessons.unit: G15-G19: Geometry and measures: measuring, mensuration and similarity
lessons.title: Similarity: lengths, areas and volumes
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a shadow tell us the height of a tower?
objectives: Prove triangles are similar and find missing lengths
Use similar triangles with parallel lines
Use area and volume scale factors for similar shapes
successCriteria: All: find a missing length using a scale factor
Most: prove two triangles are similar and use parallel lines
Some: use k² and k³ for areas and volumes
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography and physics: measuring heights with shadows

keywords.def: same shape, corresponding angles equal and sides in the same ratio
the multiplier between corresponding lengths
matching positions on two shapes

starter: A scale factor 3 enlarges a square of side 2 cm. Find the new area.

teach.heading: Similar triangles

model.problem: Triangles ABC and DEF are similar. AB = 6 cm, DE = 9 cm, BC = 8 cm. Find EF.
steps: Scale factor from ABC to DEF = 9 ÷ 6 = 1.5

teach.note: Write the correspondence in order and check the longest matches the longest. Alternatively use the ratio 6 : 9 = 8 : EF.

teach.heading: Parallel lines

model.problem: In triangle ABC, D is on AB and E on AC with DE parallel to BC. AD = 4 cm, DB = 2 cm and DE = 5 cm. Find BC.
steps: Angle A is common; angle ADE = angle ABC (corresponding)
So triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC

teach.note: The whole line AB is 6 cm. Crucial: use AB, not DB. Always state the reason for similarity: equal angles by corresponding angles, plus angle A common.

teach.heading: Hinge: parallel line

check.q: DE is parallel to BC with D on AB, E on AC. AD = 3, DB = 2 and DE = 6. Find BC.
check.why: AB = 5, scale factor 5/3, BC = 6 × 5/3 = 10. 15 uses 6 × 5/2 (DB used in place of AD); 9 uses 3 + 6.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Say why AD : DB is not the ratio of the triangles.

teach.heading: Areas and volumes

model.problem: Two similar tins have heights 8 cm and 12 cm. The smaller has a label of area 90 cm² and volume 300 cm³. Find the label area and volume of the larger.

teach.note: Revisit the table from the earlier lesson on ratios of lengths, areas and volumes. Higher tier uses these for areas and volumes.

teach.heading: Wrong scale factor

misconception.wrong: Areas are in the ratio 20 : 45 so the sides are in the ratio 20 : 45.
misconception.right: Sides are in the ratio √20 : √45 = 2 : 3 (area ratio 4 : 9).

teach.note: Always take the square root for lengths from areas, the cube root for lengths from volumes. ANSWERS: practice: 12 cm; 7.5 cm; 9 cm; 1012.5 cm³. exit: 10; 2 : 3. core: QR = 4.5 × 8 ÷ 3 = 12 cm; angle P is common, angle PST = angle PQR (corresponding) so similar (AA). extend: volume ratio 54 : 128 = 27 : 64, so length ratio 3 : 4: height 12 cm; area ratio 9 : 16 so 90 × 16/9 = 160 cm². stretch: triangles ABX and CDX similar (alternate angles) with ratio 3 : 5 so area 18 × 25/9 = 50 cm². homework: 9 m, assuming the sun's rays are parallel and both stand vertically on level ground.

practice: Triangles ABC and DEF are similar: AB = 6, DE = 9, BC = 8. Find EF.
DE is parallel to BC; AD = 4, DB = 2, DE = 5. Find BC.
Two similar triangles have areas 20 cm² and 45 cm². The smaller has a side of 6 cm. Find the matching side of the larger.
Two similar tins have heights 8 cm and 12 cm. The smaller has volume 300 cm³. Find the volume of the larger.
independent: Core: a) In triangle PQR, S is on PQ and T on PR with ST ∥ QR. PS = 3, SQ = 5 and ST = 4.5 cm. Find QR. b) Prove triangle PST is similar to triangle PQR.
Extend: Two similar vases have volumes 54 cm³ and 128 cm³. The smaller is 9 cm tall. Find the height of the larger and the surface area of the larger if the smaller has 90 cm².
Stretch: In a trapezium ABCD with AB ∥ DC, AB = 6 cm and DC = 10 cm, the diagonals meet at X. Triangle ABX has area 18 cm². Find the area of triangle CDX.
exit: DE ∥ BC with AD = 3, DB = 2, DE = 6. Find BC.
Two similar shapes have areas in the ratio 4 : 9. Write the ratio of lengths.
Big question: How can a shadow tell us the height of a tower?
lessons.homework: A 1.5 m pole casts a shadow of 2 m at the same time as a tree casts a shadow of 12 m. Find the height of the tree, and state the assumption you make.
lessons.send: SEND: redraw the two triangles separately, in the same orientation, and colour matching sides. EAL: 'corresponding', 'parallel'. Stretch: prove the intercept theorem. Higher-only: area and volume scale factors (Foundation: lengths only).

each outcome has an equal chance and cannot be predicted

starter: Write 24 out of 50 as a percentage.

teach.heading: A two-way table
teach.note: Fill in the missing entries as a class from a partial table: Boys 26, walk total 28, etc. Rows and columns both add to the totals. Ask how many girls take the bus (11) and what fraction of the walkers are boys (15/28).
bullets: Rows and columns add up

teach.heading: Frequency tree

model.problem: A class of 30 has 18 girls. 12 of the girls and 6 of the boys have a pet. Complete a frequency tree and find how many pupils have no pet.
steps: Girls: 12 have a pet so 6 do not
Boys: 6 have a pet so 6 do not

teach.note: Draw the tree: first split girls/boys, then pet/no pet. Counts on every branch; check each pair of branches adds to its parent. Ask: what fraction of pet owners are girls? 12 out of 18 = 2/3.

teach.heading: Hinge: fair selection

check.q: Which way of choosing a winner from 30 pupils is fair?
options: The first pupil to put a hand up
Writing every name on identical slips and drawing one without looking
The pupil with the highest score last week
check.why: A fair method gives every pupil the same chance. Hand-up favours the fastest; highest score is not chance; choosing a friend is biased.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask what 'random' means in the answer: no one can predict or control it.

teach.heading: Equally likely

misconception.wrong: A spinner has 3 colours so each colour has a 1/3 chance.
misconception.right: Colours are equally likely only if the sectors are the same size.

teach.note: Show a spinner with sectors of 180°, 90° and 90°. Ask which colour is most likely and why a fair spinner needs equal angles. ANSWERS: practice: 13; tree: women 48, men 32; drivers 36 + 16 = 52; heads 14, tails 6; because the people at the front are not equally likely to be chosen and may be linked. exit: 14 boys like tea (22 boys, 25 - 11 = 14); 80 total coat wearers. core: Year 11 = 50; Year 10 like 45, don't 25; Year 11 like 30, don't 20; total do not like: 45. extend: adults not buying 75 plus children 20 = 95. stretch: random choice such as draw from a hat. homework: draw names from a hat, two draws.

practice: Complete: 50 pupils, boys 26, 15 boys walk, 28 walk in total. How many girls walk?
A survey of 80 people: 3/5 are women. 3/4 of the women and half of the men drive. Complete a frequency tree and find the number who drive.
A coin is flipped 20 times and gives 14 heads. Write the frequency of heads and tails.
Explain why choosing the first 5 people in a queue is not random.
independent: Core: a) A survey of 120 pupils: 70 in Year 10; 45 of Year 10 and 30 of Year 11 like maths. Complete a two-way table. b) How many do not like maths?
Extend: 200 people attend a masjid open day: 120 are adults and 80 children. 45 adults and 60 children buy food. Draw a frequency tree and find the total who did not buy food.
Stretch: A box has red and blue counters. Describe a fair experiment to find which is more likely.
exit: A group of 40: 25 like tea. Of 18 girls, 11 like tea. How many boys like tea?
Complete a frequency tree: 100 people, 40 children; 30 children and 50 adults wear coats.
Big question: What does it mean for a choice to be fair?
lessons.homework: Design a fair way to choose 2 pupils from your class of 15 for a task, and explain why it is fair.
lessons.send: SEND: use blank trees and tables with some numbers in; colour-code rows and columns. EAL: 'frequency', 'random', 'fair'. Stretch: construct a frequency tree from percentages.

lessons.unit: P1-P9: Probability
lessons.title: Probability: expected frequency and the sum to 1
lessons.bigQuestion: Can we predict what will happen if we cannot predict one trial?
objectives: Calculate theoretical probabilities
Use P(not A) = 1 - P(A) for mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes
Find expected frequencies
successCriteria: All: calculate a probability and give it as a fraction, decimal or percentage
Most: use probabilities summing to 1 to find a missing probability
Some: estimate how many times an event occurs
lessons.smsc: Planning wisely (taking reasonable steps) and then trusting in Allah's decree: probability helps us prepare; it never replaces tawakkul.

keywords.def: a number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an event is
events that cannot happen at the same time
probability × number of trials

teach.heading: Probability facts
bullets: P(event) = number of successful outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes
All probabilities lie between 0 and 1
Probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1
P(not A) = 1 - P(A)
teach.note: Draw the 0 to 1 scale and place events: impossible, unlikely, evens, likely, certain. Mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes (one must happen, and no two can happen together) sum to 1.

teach.heading: Missing probability

model.problem: A spinner is red, blue, green or yellow. P(red) = 0.25, P(blue) = 0.4, P(green) = 0.2. Find P(yellow).

teach.note: Ask: what is P(not blue)? 0.6. Remind that the probabilities must be listed for all outcomes.

teach.heading: Expected frequency

model.problem: A fair 12-sided dice is rolled 90 times. How many multiples of 3 would you expect?

teach.note: Stress that 'expected' is an average over many trials, not a promise. Contrast with the actual result when we try it.

teach.heading: Hinge: not an event

check.q: The probability that a bus is late is 0.08. The probability it is NOT late is:
check.why: P(not late) = 1 - 0.08 = 0.92. 1.08 breaks the rule that probabilities cannot exceed 1; 0.8 subtracts wrongly.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask how many late days in 250 days (20).

teach.heading: Choosing 50:50

misconception.wrong: The chance of rain tomorrow is 'rain or no rain' so it is 1/2.
misconception.right: Outcomes are only equally likely if each has the same chance; rain and no rain generally are not.

teach.note: Contrast a coin with weather. Equally likely outcomes need a good reason. ANSWERS: practice: 0.15; 1/3 and 5/12; 20; 9/15 = 3/5. exit: 20; 0.65. core: P(fail) = 1 - 0.83 = 0.17; (0.12 + 0.31) × 600 = 258. extend: 2x + 3x + x + 0.1 = 1 so 6x = 0.9, x = 0.15. stretch: 120 failures; actual results vary randomly. homework: probabilities are between 0 and 1.

practice: P(red) = 0.25, P(blue) = 0.4, P(green) = 0.2 and the only other colour is yellow. Find P(yellow).
A fair 12-sided dice: find P(multiple of 3) and P(prime number).
The probability a train is late is 0.08. How many late trains are expected in 250 journeys?
A bag has 4 red, 5 blue, 6 green counters. Find P(not green).
independent: Core: a) The probabilities of passing a test: A grade 0.12, B grade 0.31, C grade 0.4, otherwise fail. Find P(fail). b) 600 pupils take the test: how many are expected to get an A grade or a B?
Extend: A bag has red, blue and green counters. P(red) = 2x, P(blue) = 3x and P(green) = x + 0.1. Find x.
Stretch: An event has probability 0.04 of failing. In 3000 runs, how many failures are expected? Why might the actual number differ?
exit: A fair 6-sided dice is rolled 120 times. How many 5s are expected?
P(win) = 0.35. Find P(not win).
Big question: Can we predict what will happen if we cannot predict one trial?
lessons.homework: Explain why the probability of an event can never be -0.2 or 1.4.
lessons.send: SEND: draw the 0-1 probability line; give a template for each calculation. EAL: 'likely', 'unlikely', 'expected'. Stretch: forming and solving equations from probability sums.

lessons.unit: P1-P9: Probability
lessons.title: Relative frequency and the effect of sample size
lessons.bigQuestion: How many trials do we need before we can trust an experiment?
objectives: Calculate relative frequency
Estimate probability from experimental data
Explain why more trials give more reliable estimates
successCriteria: All: calculate a relative frequency
Most: compare a relative frequency with the theoretical probability
Some: explain why larger samples give better estimates and combine results
lessons.smsc: Honesty in reporting results: do not cherry-pick the data.

keywords.def: frequency ÷ total number of trials
one go at an experiment
not fair; some outcomes more likely than others

starter: A coin is flipped 10 times and lands heads 7 times. Write this as a fraction.

teach.heading: Relative frequency
bullets: Relative frequency = number of times ÷ number of trials
It estimates the probability when outcomes are not equally likely
More trials give a better estimate
Results vary: no trial is guaranteed to match the theory
teach.note: Show the coin-flip results as a table: after 10 flips 7 heads (0.7), after 50 flips 29 heads (0.58), after 200 flips 106 (0.53), after 1000 flips 512 (0.512). The estimates move towards 0.5.

teach.heading: Coin experiment
teach.note: Ask pupils to say what they notice. Larger samples give estimates nearer to 0.5. This is the idea behind the law of large numbers; no need to name it, but mention it. Ask them to predict the value at 10 000 flips.
bullets: Larger sample, closer to 0.5

teach.heading: A biased spinner

model.problem: A spinner is spun 200 times and lands on red 62 times. Estimate P(red) and the number of reds in 1000 spins.

teach.note: The estimate comes from the data and is more reliable with more spins. Compare with 1/4 if the spinner were fair: 0.25 is very different, so it may be biased.

teach.heading: Hinge: gambler's fallacy

check.q: A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. The probability of heads on the next flip is:
check.why: Each flip is independent: the coin has no memory. Choosing 'less' expects it to balance out.

teach.note: Whiteboards. This is the gambler's fallacy; use it to link to independence.

teach.heading: Equalising

misconception.wrong: After 10 flips we should have exactly 5 heads and 5 tails.
misconception.right: Over a small number of trials the results are usually uneven; over many trials the relative frequency approaches 0.5.

teach.note: Ask pupils to flip a coin ten times, then pool results from the whole class: closer to even. ANSWERS: practice: 0.24 against 1/6 ≈ 0.167, so possibly biased; 240; Student B, because more trials; (9 + 190) ÷ 520 ≈ 0.383. exit: 0.25; larger samples are more reliable. core: 34/80 = 0.425; 0.425 × 500 ≈ 213. extend: 0.56 is a little high but within normal variation for 100 flips; flip more times and combine; x = 1 - 0.77 = 0.23 and 0.23 × 600 = 138. homework: results vary but the combined sample is nearer 0.5.

practice: A dice is rolled 300 times and gives 72 sixes. Find the relative frequency of a six and compare with the theoretical probability.
Estimate the number of sixes in 1000 rolls of this dice.
Student A: 20 trials, 9 red. Student B: 500 trials, 190 red. Whose estimate is more reliable, and why?
Combine the two sets of results to give a best estimate of P(red).
independent: Core: a) A drawing pin lands point up 34 times in 80 throws. Estimate P(point up). b) Estimate how many point-up results in 500 throws.
Extend: A coin is flipped 100 times and lands heads 56 times. Decide whether this is evidence that the coin is biased, and what you would do next.
Stretch: A spinner has three colours with relative frequencies 0.31, 0.46 and x after 1500 spins. Find x and the expected number of the third colour in 600 spins.
exit: A dice is rolled 60 times; a 4 appears 15 times. Find the relative frequency.
Why is 1000 trials better than 10?
Big question: How many trials do we need before we can trust an experiment?
lessons.homework: Flip a coin 20 times at home and record the results. Calculate the relative frequency of heads. Then pool with a friend's results: what happens?
lessons.send: SEND: use a recording sheet with tally and totals; use a calculator for division. EAL: 'relative', 'trial', 'biased'. Stretch: standard error idea, why the spread decreases with n.

lessons.unit: P1-P9: Probability
lessons.title: Sample spaces, listing outcomes and Venn diagrams
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we be sure we have counted every possible outcome?
objectives: List outcomes systematically
Use sample space grids
Use Venn diagrams and set notation for probability
successCriteria: All: list all outcomes for two events
Most: use a sample space to find a probability
Some: complete a Venn diagram and use set notation
lessons.smsc: Thoroughness in counting; being methodical in a decision.

keywords.def: a list or table of all possible outcomes
A ∪ B: in A or B or both
A ∩ B: in both A and B

starter: Find the highest common factor of 12 and 18.
How many outcomes when two coins are flipped?

teach.heading: Sample space: sum of two dice
teach.note: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. Count the 7s: 6 of them so P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6. P(sum ≥ 10) = 6/36. P(a prime sum): 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 occur 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15 times so 15/36 = 5/12. Ask pupils why 1 to 12 sums are not equally likely.
bullets: 36 outcomes, not 11

teach.heading: Systematic listing

model.problem: Three coins are flipped. List all the outcomes and find P(exactly two heads).
steps: Fix the first coin: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT
Then fix the first as T: THH, THT, TTH, TTT
Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH = 3

teach.note: The systematic method guarantees none are missed. The number of outcomes is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

teach.heading: Venn diagram

model.problem: In a class of 40, 22 play football (F), 18 play cricket (C), 7 play both and 7 play neither. Find P(football only), P(C ∪ F) and P(F ∩ C).

teach.note: Start with the overlap. Check the four regions sum to 40. Notation: ∪ is 'or', ∩ is 'and', A' is 'not A'.

teach.heading: Hinge: Venn notation

check.q: What does A ∩ B mean?
options: in A or B or both
check.why: A ∩ B is the intersection: both A and B. The union A ∪ B is 'or'.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Show with a Venn diagram: intersection is the overlap.

teach.heading: Venn regions for the class
teach.note: Use the table in place of a diagram if you cannot show a picture: ask pupils to draw the Venn from it. They should sum to 40. Use it to ask P(F') = 18/40. ANSWERS: practice: 6 outcomes: 1H, 1T, 2H, 2T, 3H, 3T; 5/36 and 6/36 = 1/6; Venn: French only 9, both 5, Spanish only 7, neither 9 so P(neither) = 3/10; 3/10 and 21/30 = 7/10. exit: 1/36; 3. core: 9 outcomes (RR, RB, RG, BR, BB, BG, GR, GB, GG); 3/9 = 1/3; both = 28 + 25 - 41 = 12; extend: P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.15 = 0.75 and P(neither) = 0.25. stretch: 6/36 against 1/36. homework: 1/6 against 1/36.

practice: List all outcomes for a spinner with 1, 2, 3 and a coin with H, T.
Use the sum grid to find P(sum = 8) and P(double).
In a group of 30: 14 study French, 12 study Spanish, 5 study both. Complete a Venn diagram and find P(neither).
Find P(French only) and P(French or Spanish).
independent: Core: a) A bag has red, blue and green counters. Two are taken in order with replacement. List all outcomes. b) Find P(same colour) if each colour is equally likely.
Extend: In a survey of 50, 28 have a tablet (T), 25 have a phone (P) and 9 have neither. Find the number with both and draw a Venn diagram.
Stretch: Venn diagram: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.15. Find P(A ∪ B) and P(neither).
exit: Find P(sum is 12) when two dice are rolled.
In a Venn diagram of 20 people, 8 are in A only, 5 in both, 4 in B only. How many are in neither?
Big question: How can we be sure we have counted every possible outcome?
lessons.homework: Show that when two fair dice are thrown, the probability that the total is 7 is greater than the probability that it is 12.
lessons.send: SEND: give the sample space grid partly filled; use coloured counters in a Venn. EAL: 'outcome', 'union', 'intersection'. Stretch: inclusion-exclusion formula P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B).

lessons.unit: P1-P9: Probability
lessons.title: Tree diagrams: independent events
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we find the chance of two things both happening?
objectives: Draw a tree diagram for independent events
Multiply along branches and add between branches
Use 'at least one' and state assumptions
successCriteria: All: draw a tree for two independent events and read off probabilities
Most: calculate 'exactly one' and 'at least one'
Some: state and challenge the assumption of independence
lessons.smsc: Reasoning about possibilities; avoiding assumptions that are not justified.

keywords.def: one event does not change the probability of the other
a diagram with branches for each outcome and probabilities on the branches
multiply probabilities for independent events

teach.heading: Rules for tree diagrams
bullets: Probabilities on branches from one point add to 1
Multiply along branches for 'and'
Add the results for 'or' (different routes)
Independent events: the same numbers on every second branch
teach.note: Draw a tree on the board for a penalty taker scoring with probability 0.8 twice. Establish before calculating: what does it mean for the shots to be independent? (the first result does not alter the second).

teach.heading: Two penalties

model.problem: A player scores each penalty with probability 0.8, independently. Find P(both), P(exactly one) and P(at least one).
steps: Score S 0.8, miss M 0.2 on each branch

teach.note: Check that all four routes sum to 1: 0.64 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.04. 'At least one' is almost always easiest as 1 - none.

teach.heading: Hinge: and rule

check.q: P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent. P(A and B) is:
check.why: 0.6 × 0.5 = 0.3. 1.1 adds; 0.55 is the mean; 0.1 subtracts.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for P(A or B) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.8.

teach.heading: Rain on two days

model.problem: P(rain Saturday) = 0.4 and P(rain Sunday) = 0.3. Assume independence. Find P(rain on both), P(rain on neither) and P(rain on exactly one day).

teach.note: Discuss the assumption: weather on consecutive days is probably not independent. Ask what difference it would make.

teach.heading: Adding along branches
teach.note: Ask: could the answer be bigger than either probability? Both events together are less likely than each alone. ANSWERS: practice: 1/36 and 11/36; 0.02 and 0.72; 1/8; 0.42 and 0.88. exit: 0.09 and 0.42; drawing a second card without replacing the first. core: P(different) = 0.3 × 0.7 + 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42; P(at least one red) = 1 - 0.49 = 0.51. extend: works = 0.95 × 0.9 = 0.855; at least one fails = 0.145. stretch: 0.9^5 ≈ 0.590. homework: 1 - 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.91, assuming independence.

practice: Two dice are rolled: find P(two sixes) and P(at least one six).
P(late on Monday) = 0.2 and P(late on Tuesday) = 0.1, independent. Find P(late on both days) and P(late on neither).
A fair coin is flipped three times. Find P(all heads).
P(pass theory test) = 0.7 and P(pass practical) = 0.6, independent. Find P(pass both) and P(pass at least one).
independent: Core: a) A bag has 3 red and 7 blue counters. One is taken and replaced; then another. Draw a tree and find P(two different colours). b) P(at least one red).
Extend: A machine's two parts fail independently with probabilities 0.05 and 0.1. Find P(machine works if both parts are needed) and P(at least one fails).
Stretch: P(a bus is late) = 0.1 each day for 5 days. Find P(on time all 5 days) to 3 s.f.
exit: P(win) = 0.3 in a game. Two games are played independently. Find P(win both) and P(win exactly one).
State one situation where two events are not independent.
Big question: How do we find the chance of two things both happening?
lessons.homework: Two friends each have a 0.7 probability of arriving on time to class. Find the probability that at least one is on time. State your assumption.
lessons.send: SEND: provide blank tree templates and write the multiplications beside the branches. EAL: 'at least one', 'independent'. Stretch: 5-day questions using (1 - p)^5.

lessons.unit: P1-P9: Probability
lessons.title: Tree diagrams: dependent events and without replacement
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does taking a counter out change the next probability?
objectives: Recognise events that are not independent
Draw trees for selection without replacement
Calculate probabilities such as 'at least one' with changing denominators
successCriteria: All: write the probabilities after one selection without replacement
Most: complete a tree and find probabilities of combined events
Some: solve equations from dependent probability statements
lessons.smsc: Fairness and honesty about assumptions: random selection and sampling without bias.

keywords.def: the probability of the second event depends on the first
the item is not put back
the item is put back

teach.heading: Without replacement

model.problem: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue counters. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(RR), P(BB) and P(different colours).
steps: After a red: R 4/7, B 3/7. After a blue: R 5/7, B 2/7

teach.note: The total reduces by one on the second branch. Check the sum: 20/56 + 6/56 + 30/56 = 1. Ask what happens to the second branch if the counter had been replaced (the same numbers as the first branch).

teach.heading: Hinge: second pick

check.q: From 5 red and 3 blue counters, a red is taken and not replaced. P(the next is red) is:
check.why: 4 reds left out of 7 counters. 5/8 ignores the removal; 5/7 removes only from the total; 4/8 removes only from the numerator.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask for P(blue next) (3/7).

teach.heading: At least one

model.problem: A box has 12 pens, 3 of which are faulty. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(at least one faulty).

teach.note: Show the complement method again. Check by adding up the other routes: 3/12 × 2/11 + 3/12 × 9/11 + 9/12 × 3/11 = 6/132 + 27/132 + 27/132 = 60/132 = 5/11.

teach.heading: Same fractions both times

misconception.wrong: P(RR) = 5/8 × 5/8 because the probability of red is 5/8.
misconception.right: Without replacement P(RR) = 5/8 × 4/7: the bag has changed.

teach.note: Ask: 'what is in the bag now?' every time before writing the second branch.

teach.heading: Dependent tree: method
cycle: Draw first branches with probabilities adding to 1
Update numerator and denominator for the second branches
Add routes for 'or'; check the total is 1
teach.note: Use as a checklist. Ask pupils to say which step is different from the independent case (the third). Mention in exam answers state the numbers left in the bag. ANSWERS: practice: 1/3, 2/15, 8/15; 1/22 and 5/11; with replacement P(RR) = 9/25 = 0.36 which is higher; 5/8 × 4/7 × 3/6 = 5/28. exit: 4/10 × 3/9 = 2/15; the bag has changed (4 reds out of 7). core: P(both mint) = 3/8 × 2/7 = 3/28; exactly one = 2 × 3/8 × 5/7 = 15/28; random selection, each equally likely. extend: P(at least one boy) = 1 - 12/20 × 11/19 = 1 - 132/380 = 62/95. stretch: 3/(n + 3) × 2/(n + 2) = 1/5 gives 30 = n² + 5n + 6 so n² + 5n - 24 = 0, (n + 8)(n - 3) = 0, n = 3. homework: 6/10 × 4/9 × 2 = 48/90 = 8/15.

practice: A bag has 6 red and 4 yellow counters. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(RR), P(YY) and P(different).
A box has 12 pens, 3 faulty. Two are taken without replacement. Find P(both faulty) and P(at least one faulty).
Repeat question 1 with replacement and compare P(RR).
From 5 red and 3 blue counters, three are taken without replacement. Find P(all red).
independent: Core: a) 8 sweets: 3 mint and 5 fruit. Two are eaten at random. Find P(both mint) and P(exactly one mint). b) Comment on the assumptions.
Extend: A class of 20 has 12 girls. Two pupils are chosen at random. Find P(at least one boy).
Stretch: A bag has 3 red and n blue counters. Two counters are taken without replacement. The probability both are red is 1/5. Show that n² + 5n - 24 = 0 and find n.
exit: From a pack of 10 cards, 4 are hearts. Two are drawn without replacement. Find P(both hearts).
Why is P(second red) not 5/8 after a red was removed from 5R, 3B?
Big question: Why does taking a counter out change the next probability?
lessons.homework: Pick two pupils from a class of 10 (6 girls, 4 boys) for a role. Find the probability that one boy and one girl are chosen.
lessons.send: SEND: use physical counters in a bag and update the numbers after each pick. EAL: 'with replacement', 'without replacement'. Stretch: three-stage trees and algebraic bag problems. Higher-only: three-stage trees and algebraic bag problems (Foundation: two-stage trees).

lessons.unit: P1-P9: Probability
lessons.title: Conditional probability
lessons.bigQuestion: If we know something has already happened, how does that change the probability?
objectives: Use two-way tables for conditional probability
Use Venn diagrams and tree diagrams for conditional probability
Understand that P(A given B) is different from P(B given A)
successCriteria: All: read a conditional probability from a two-way table
Most: use a Venn diagram or tree for a conditional probability
Some: explain the difference between P(A | B) and P(B | A)
lessons.crossCurricular: Medicine and quality control: tests and screening
lessons.smsc: Careful reasoning: claims about 'given that' must be checked against the right group.

keywords.def: the probability of an event given that another has happened
restricts the group we look at
the probability of A given B

starter: A two-way table has 30 pupils in Year 11, of which 16 walk. Write 16 out of 30 in simplest form.
Find P(second red) from 5R, 3B after one red is removed.
Write 7/22 as a decimal to 2 d.p.

teach.heading: A two-way table for conditional probability
teach.note: Higher only. 'Given that' tells us which group is the whole. P(walks | Year 11) = 16/30 = 8/15. P(Year 11 | bus) = 14/32 = 7/16. Ask: why are these different from 16/60 and 14/60?
bullets: The 'given' group is the denominator

teach.heading: A Venn diagram

model.problem: In a class of 40: 15 football only, 7 both, 11 cricket only, 7 neither. Find P(cricket | football) and P(football | cricket).

teach.note: The two conditional probabilities are not equal. The denominator is the group we are told about.

teach.heading: Hinge: the denominator

check.q: From the table, P(Year 11 | bus) is:
check.why: We are told the pupil takes the bus: 32 pupils, and 14 of these are in Year 11. 14/30 uses the wrong group; 14/60 ignores the condition.

teach.note: Whiteboards. Ask what 14/30 means (P(bus | Year 11)).

teach.heading: A tree with a condition

model.problem: Counters: 6 red and 4 yellow. Two are taken without replacement. Given that the counters are different colours, find the probability that the first was red.

teach.note: Formula: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B). The condition removes the routes RR and YY from the sample space. Symmetry argument gives the same answer.

teach.heading: Reversing the condition

misconception.right: In general P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A) because the denominators differ.

teach.note: Use the football / cricket example: 7/22 against 7/18. ANSWERS: practice: 12/28 = 3/7; 5/14 and 5/12; 4/9; different denominators (32 against 30). exit: 12/30 = 2/5; 4/14 = 2/7. core: P(neither | not French) = 9/16; flagged = 285, faulty flagged 95, so 1/3. extend: from the table method; P(A | B) = n(A ∩ B) ÷ n(B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B). stretch: in 10 000: 100 faulty, 90 flagged; 9900 good, 495 flagged; P = 90/585 = 2/13 ≈ 0.154. homework: written explanation.

practice: Using the table: P(a Year 10 pupil | walks).
In a group of 30: French only 9, both 5, Spanish only 7, neither 9. Find P(Spanish | French) and P(French | Spanish).
